'''Takeminakata''' (タケミナカタ), also known as '''Minakatatomi''' or '''Takeminakatatomi''', is a ''[[kami]]'' in [[Japanese mythology]]. Also known as {{nihongo|'''Suwa {{ill|Myōjin|en|Myōjin|qid=Q5369590|lt=Myōjin}}'''|諏訪明神 / 諏方明神}} or {{nihongo|'''Suwa Daimyōjin'''|諏訪大明神 / 諏方大明神}} after [[Suwa-taisha|Suwa Grand Shrine]] (Suwa Taisha) in {{ill|Nagano Prefecture|en|Nagano Prefecture|qid=Q127877|lt=Nagano Prefecture}} in which he is enshrined alongside his consort [[Yasakatome]], Takeminakata is historically worshiped as a god of {{ill|List of wind deities|en|en:List of wind deities|qid=Q51845481|lt=wind}}, {{ill|List of water deities|en|List of water deities|qid=Q13416336|lt=water}} and {{ill|List of nature deities|en|en:List of nature deities|qid=Q6630292|lt=agriculture}}, as well as a patron of {{ill|List of hunting deities|en|en:List of hunting deities|qid=Q6623822|lt=hunting}} and {{ill|List of war deities|en|List of war deities|qid=Q1752560|lt=warfare}}, in which capacity he enjoyed a particularly fervent cult from various {{ill|Samurai|en|Samurai|qid=Q38142|lt=Samurai}} clans during the medieval period such as the {{ill|Hōjō clan|en|Hōjō clan|qid=Q834364|lt=Hōjō}} or the [[Takeda clan|Takeda]]. Takeminakata was also held to be the mythical ancestor of certain families who once served at the shrine as priests, foremost among them being the [[Suwa clan]], the high priests of the Upper Shrine of Suwa who were also revered as [[Arahitogami|living]] [[Shintai|vessels]] of the god.

Whereas in the ''[[Kojiki]]'' (ca. 712 CE) and later derivative accounts, Takeminakata appears as one of the sons of the god [[Ōkuninushi]] who fled to {{ill|Lake Suwa|en|Lake Suwa|qid=Q1206692|lt=Lake Suwa}} after being defeated by the warrior god [[Takemikazuchi]], other myths (mostly of medieval origin) instead offer alternative explanations regarding the god of Suwa Shrine's origins and identity, portraying him either as an interloper who conquered Suwa by defeating the local ''kami'' of the region, as a king from {{ill|India|en|India|qid=Q668|lt=India}} who [[Honji suijaku|manifested]] in Japan, or as a {{ill|Snake worship|en|Snake worship|qid=Q3249489|lt=snake}} or {{ill|Japanese dragon|en|Japanese dragon|qid=Q2366503|lt=dragon}} deity.

==Name==
[[File:Suwa Hosshō Banner - 諏訪法性旗.png|thumb|right|135px|Reproduction of {{ill|Takeda Shingen|en|Takeda Shingen|qid=Q276404|lt=Takeda Shingen}}'s Suwa Hosshō banner (諏訪法性旗). The inscription reads: ''[[:wikt:南無#Japanese|Namu]] Suwa Nangū Hosshō Kamishimo'' (or ''Jōge'') ''Daimyōjin'' (南無諏方南宮法性上下大明神)]]
The god is named 'Takeminakata-no-Kami' ({{nihongo2|建御名方神}}) in both the ''[[Kojiki]]'' (ca. 712 CE) and the ''[[Kujiki|''Sendai Kuji Hongi'']]'' (ca. 807-936 CE).<ref name="Hongi2">{{cite web|title=先代舊事本紀卷第四|url=http://miko.org/~uraki/kuon/furu/text/sendaikuji/sendaikuji04.htm|website=私本 先代舊事本紀}}</ref><ref name="Hongi">''Sendai Kuji Hongi'', Book 4 (先代舊事本紀 巻第四), in {{cite book|editor=Keizai Zasshisha|title=Kokushi-taikei, vol. 7 (国史大系 第7巻)|date=1898|publisher=Keizai Zasshisha|pages=243–244|url=http://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/991097/136}}</ref> Variants of the name found in the imperially commissioned [[Rikkokushi|national histories]] and other literary sources include the following:<ref>{{Cite web|title=南方刀美神社|url=http://21coe.kokugakuin.ac.jp/db/jinja/240101.html|access-date=2020-12-05|website=神道・神社史料集成 (Shinto Jinja Database)|publisher=Kokugakuin University}}</ref>

* Minakatatomi-no-Kami (南方刀美神)
* Minakatatomi-no-Mikoto-no-Kami (御名方富命神)
* Takeminakatatomi-no-Mikoto (健御名方富命 / 建御名方富命)
* Takeminakatatomi-no-Mikoto-no-Kami (建御名方富命神)

The etymology of the name '(Take)minakata(tomi)' is unclear. While most commentators seem to agree that ''take-'' (and probably ''-tomi'') are honorifics, they differ in how to interpret the other components of the name. Some of the proposed solutions are as follows.

*The {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|qid=Q184963|lt=Edo period}} ''{{ill|Kokugaku|en|Kokugaku|qid=Q855159|lt=Kokugaku}}'' scholar {{ill|Motoori Norinaga|en|Motoori Norinaga|qid=Q384647|lt=Motoori Norinaga}}<ref name="Norinaga2">Motoori, Norinaga (1937). [http://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/1109355/81 古事記傳 (''Kojiki-den''), vol. 14] in Motoori Toyokai (ed.), ''Motoori Norinaga Zenshū'' (本居宣長全集), vol. 2. Tokyo: Yoshikawa Kōbunkan. p. 675. (Original work written 1764–1798)</ref> explained both ''take-'' (建) and ''mi-'' (御) as honorifics (称名 ''tatae-na''), with ''kata'' (方) as yet another ''tatae-na'' meaning "hard" or "firm" (堅). [[:en:Basil Chamberlain|Basil Chamberlain]] followed Motoori's lead and rendered the god's name as 'Brave-August-Name-Firm' in his translation of the ''Kojiki''.<ref name="Chamberlain">Chamberlain, Basil (trans.) (1882). [http://sacred-texts.com/shi/kj/kj039.htm Section XXXII.—Abdication of the Deity Master-of-the-Great-Land.] ''A translation of the "Ko-ji-ki" or Records of Ancient Matters.'' Yokohama: Lane, Crawford & Co.</ref>
*[[:ja:太田亮|Ōta Akira]] (1926) interpreted ''take-'', ''mi-'' and ''-tomi'' as honorifics and took ''Nakata'' (名方) to be a place name: Nakata District ([[:ja:名方郡|名方郡]]) in {{ill|Awa Province (Tokushima)|en|Awa Province (Tokushima)|qid=Q907457|lt=Awa Province}} (modern {{ill|Ishii, Tokushima|en|Ishii, Tokushima|qid=Q1205943|lt=Ishii}}, {{ill|Tokushima Prefecture|en|Tokushima Prefecture|qid=Q160734|lt=Tokushima Prefecture}}), where [https://www.google.co.jp/maps/place/%E3%80%92779-3200+Tokushima-ken,+My%C5%8Dzai-gun,+Ishii-ch%C5%8D,+Urash%C5%8D,+Suwa%E2%88%92213%E2%88%921,+%E5%A4%9A%E7%A5%81%E5%BE%A1%E5%A5%88%E5%88%80%E5%BC%A5%E7%A5%9E%E7%A4%BE/@34.0723826,134.4092873,17z/data=!3m1!4b1!4m5!3m4!1s0x35530a6f7db45037:0x3b0f62dd7dc4f1db!8m2!3d34.0723861!4d134.4114833 Takeminatomi Shrine] (多祁御奈刀弥神社) stands.<ref>Ōta (1926). p. 8.</ref> [[:ja:大和岩雄|Ōwa Iwao]] (1990) suggests that the presence of [[Azumi people]] in both Awa and Shinano, as well as the possible connection between the Azumi and the Lower Shrine of Suwa, may explain the similarity between 'Takeminakata(tomi)' and 'Takeminatomi'.<ref>Ōwa (1990). pp. 214–216.</ref>
*''Minakata'' has also been linked to the [[Munakata Taisha|Munakata]] (宗像) of [[Kyushu]].<ref name="Yoshii">{{Citation|title = Takeminakata-no-Kami (建御名方神)|author=Yoshii, Iwao|encyclopedia = Encyclopedia Nipponica|year=1994 |volume=14|publisher=Shōgakukan|isbn=978-4-09-526114-0}}</ref> [[:ja:松岡静雄|Matsuoka Shizuo]] (1936) interpreted Minakatatomi as originally being a goddess – citing the fact that the deities of Munakata shrine were female – that was later conflated with the male god Takeminakata.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Matsuoka|first1=Shizuo|title=Minzokugaku yori mitaru Azuma-uta to Sakimori-uta (民族學より見たる東歌と防人歌)|date=1936|publisher=Ōokayama-shoten|pages=197–199|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=QLb0QBVHZW8C}}</ref>
*Another explanation proposes ''minakata'' to mean "south(ern)" (南方).<ref>Miyaji (1931). p. 10.</ref> A variant of this hypothesis sees the name as hinting at a connection between the god and {{ill|Metalworking|en|Metalworking|qid=Q953045|lt=Metalworking}}, in which the southern direction is important: [[:ja:真弓常忠|Mayumi Tsunetada]] (1981) for instance proposed that Takeminakata's name refers to the southern pillar of a ''takadono'' (a high-roofed house housing a ''{{ill|Tatara (furnace)|en|Tatara (furnace)|qid=Q3131218|lt=tatara}}'' furnace).<ref>{{Cite book|title = Nihon kodai saishi to tetsu (日本古代祭祀と鉄)|last1=Mayumi|first1=Tsunetada|publisher=Gakuseisha|page=110|year=1981}}</ref> Gustav Heldt's translation of the ''Kojiki'' (2014), where the name is translated as 'Brave Southward Smelter', follows this interpretation.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Heldt |first1=Gustav |title=The Kojiki: An Account of Ancient Matters |date=2014 |publisher=Columbia University Press |pages=46, 210 |isbn=9780231163880 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=RAMZBQAAQBAJ}}</ref>
*Yet another theory interprets ''mi(na)-'' to mean "water" (水), pointing to the god being a [[:en:Water deity|Water deity]] perhaps associated with {{ill|Lake Suwa|en|Lake Suwa|qid=Q1206692|lt=Lake Suwa}}.<ref name="Yamaguchi">{{cite book|author=Yamaguchi, Yoshinori and Kōnoshi, Takamitsu (eds.)|title=Shinpen nihon koten bungaku zenshū, vol. 1. Kojiki ''(新編日本古典文学全集 (1) 古事記)''|date=1997|publisher=[[Shōgakukan]]|isbn=978-4-09-658001-1|pages=107–111}}</ref><ref name="Muraoka">Muraoka (1969). pp. 14–16.</ref><ref name="Okada">Okada, Yoneo (1966). ''Zenkoku jinja saijin goshintokki'' (全国神社祭神御神徳記), quoted in Muraoka (1969). p. 14.</ref><ref name="Miyasaka31">Miyasaka, Mitsuaki (1987). "Kyodai naru kami no kuni. Suwa-shinko no tokushitsu (強大なる神の国―諏訪信仰の特質)." In Ueda; Gorai; Ōbayashi; Miyasaka, M.; Miyasaka, Y. p. 31.</ref> The full name is thought to derive from a word denoting a body of water or a waterside region such as 水潟 (''minakata'', "{{ill|Lagoon|en|Lagoon|qid=Q187223|lt=Lagoon}}" or "{{ill|Inlet|en|Inlet|qid=Q1172599|lt=Inlet}}")<ref name="Yoshii" /><ref name="Okada" /><ref name="Miyasaka31" /> or 水県 (''mi(na)-'' "water" + ''agata'' "country(side)").<ref name="Muraoka" />
*An alternative explanation for the word ''-tomi'' (as well as the ''-tome'' in '[[Yasakatome]]', the name of this god's consort) is to link it with dialectal words for "snake" (''tomi'', ''tobe'', or ''tōbe''), thereby seeing the name as hinting to the god being a kind of {{ill|Snake worship|en|Snake worship|qid=Q3249489|lt=serpentine}} water deity (''[[mizuchi]]'').<ref>Tomiku, Takashi (1970). ''Himiko'' (卑弥呼). Gakuseisha. p. 48, cited in Kanai (1982). p. 6.</ref>

===''Suwa Daimyōjin''===
{{see also|Myōjin}}

During the medieval and early modern periods, the god enshrined in [[Suwa-taisha|Suwa Grand Shrine]] – specifically, in the Upper Shrine (''Kamisha'') located southeast of {{ill|Lake Suwa|en|Lake Suwa|qid=Q1206692|lt=Lake Suwa}} – was popularly known as ''Suwa Daimyōjin'' ({{nihongo2|諏訪大明神}} / 諏方大明神) or ''Suwa Myōjin'' ({{nihongo2|諏訪明神}}), a name also applied via {{ill|Metonymy|en|Metonymy|qid=Q41966|lt=Metonymy}} to the shrine itself. The name '(Take)minakata(tomi)' was rarely used, if at all, during this period: indeed, medieval documents from Suwa Shrine simply refer to the god as ''sonshin'' / ''sonjin'' (尊神, "revered deity") or ''{{ill|Myōjin|en|Myōjin|qid=Q5369590|lt=Myōjin}}'' (明神, "bright deity" or "manifest deity").<ref>Suwa Shishi Hensan Iinkai, ed. (1995). p. 688.</ref> This however is hardly unusual, as before the early modern period use of titles such as ''myōjin'' or ''[[gongen]]'' for various gods and their shrines were so widespread that these deities were rarely referred to by their classical names.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Nakamura|first1=Issei|title=平安期における大明神号の成立とその意義 (The Formation and Significance of the Title Daimyoujin in the Heian Period)|journal=The Bukkyo University Graduate School Review. Compiled by the Graduate School of Literature.|date=2009-03-01|issue=37|page=74|url=http://archives.bukkyo-u.ac.jp/repository/baker/rid_DB003700003047}}</ref>

Other epithets applied to the Suwa deity include ''Nangū Daimyōjin'' (南宮大明神, "Daimyōjin of the Southern Shrine (''Nangū'')"), ''Hosshō Daimyōjin'' (法性大明神, "{{ill|Reality in Buddhism|en|Reality in Buddhism|qid=Q5551108|lt=Dharma-Nature}} Daimyōjin"), a combination of the two such as ''Nangū Hosshō Daimyōjin'' (南宮法性大明神), or ''Suwa Hosshō Kamishimo'' (or ''Jōge'') ''Daimyōjin'' (諏訪法性上下大明神, "Dharma-Nature Daimyōjin of the Upper and Lower Suwa [Shrines]").<ref>{{Cite book|last=Miyaji|first=Naokazu|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=UHYSgY4lTZcC|title=諏訪史 第2巻 後編 (Suwa-shi, vol. 2, part 2)|publisher=Shinano Kyōikukai Suwa Bukai|year=1937|pages=86}}</ref> Some of the war banners used by {{ill|Sengoku period|en|Sengoku period|qid=Q204023|lt=Sengoku}} ''[[:en:Daimyō|Daimyō]]'' {{ill|Takeda Shingen|en|Takeda Shingen|qid=Q276404|lt=Takeda Shingen}} (a devotee of the god) for instance contain the inscription ''Suwa Nangū Hosshō Kamishimo'' / ''Jōge Daimyōjin'' (諏訪南宮法性上下大明神 / 諏方南宮法性上下大明神).<ref name="Guide">{{cite web|title=山梨の文化財ガイド (Guide to Cultural Assets of Yamanashi)|url=https://www.pref.yamanashi.jp/gakujutu/bunkazaihogo/bunkazai_data/yamanashinobunkazai_rekishishiryou002.html|website=Official website of Yamanashi Prefecture|access-date=January 28, 2017|archive-date=May 6, 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180506204347/http://www.pref.yamanashi.jp/gakujutu/bunkazaihogo/bunkazai_data/yamanashinobunkazai_rekishishiryou002.html|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>Miyaji (1931b). pp. 86–89.</ref> A {{ill|Hanging scroll|en|Hanging scroll|qid=Q2188827|lt=Hanging scroll}} given by {{ill|Emperor Go-Nara|en|Emperor Go-Nara|qid=Q349467|lt=Emperor Go-Nara}} (reigned 1526–1557) to the Upper Shrine in 1553 ({{ill|Tenbun|en|Tenbun|qid=Q1192853|lt=Tenbun}} 22), written in the emperor's own calligraphy, refers to the god as ''Suwa Shōichii Nangū Hossho Daimyōjin'' (諏方正一位南宮法性大明神, "Dharma-Nature Daimyōjin of the Suwa ''Nangū'', of [[Ritsuryō#Establishment of court Rank|Upper First Rank]]").<ref name="miyasakayusho">{{Cite book|last=Miyasaka|first=Yūshō|title=御柱祭と諏訪大社 (Onbashira-sai to Suwa taisha)|publisher=Chikuma Shobō|year=1987|pages=162–164|chapter=神と仏の融合ー密教思想からの解釈 (Kami to hotoke no yūgō: mikkyō shisō kara no kaishaku)}}</ref>

[[File:Size of Lake Suwa.png|thumb|left|300px|Comparison of {{ill|Lake Suwa|en|Lake Suwa|qid=Q1206692|lt=Lake Suwa}} at its prime ([[Kofun period|Kofun]] - {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|qid=Q193292|lt=Heian}} periods) with its current size. Also shown are two of the four shrines that comprise [[Suwa-taisha|Suwa Taisha]] (''Kamisha Honmiya'' and ''Shimosha Akimiya'').]]
A number of explanations have been proposed for the origin of the term ''Nangū.'' One theory posits it to refer to the geographical location of the Upper Suwa Shrine, which is located ''southeast'' of Lake Suwa, at the ''southern'' half of Shinano Province, while another claims it to be derived from 'Minakatatomi' (南方刀美), one of the variant names for the deity, with ''minakata'' being apparently understood to mean "south(ern)" (cf. etymology of 'Takeminakata' above).<ref>Miyaji (1937). pp. 23-24.</ref> The term has also been interpreted to come from the medieval belief that the Suwa deity was the guardian of the ''south'' side of the [[Kyoto Imperial Palace|imperial palace]]<ref>Takei (1999). pp. 130, 142.</ref> or the [[Shinbutsu-shūgō|Shinto-Buddhist]] concept that the god is an enlightened being who [[Honji suijaku|manifested]] in our world, which in {{ill|Buddhist cosmology|en|Buddhist cosmology|qid=Q1308653|lt=Buddhist cosmology}} is the ''southern'' continent of {{ill|Jambudvīpa|en|Jambudvīpa|qid=Q1586228|lt=Jambudvīpa}}.<ref name="miyasakayusho" />

Aside from Suwa Shrine, ''Nangū'' was also applied to Kanayamahiko Shrine in {{ill|Mino Province|en|Mino Province|qid=Q864156|lt=Mino Province}} (modern [[Nangū Taisha]] in {{ill|Gifu Prefecture|en|Gifu Prefecture|qid=Q131277|lt=Gifu Prefecture}}) and [[Aekuni Shrine]] (南宮大菩薩, ''Nangū Daibosatsu'') in {{ill|Iga Province|en|Iga Province|qid=Q1047128|lt=Iga Province}} (modern {{ill|Mie Prefecture|en|Mie Prefecture|qid=Q128196|lt=Mie Prefecture}}). A song in the late {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|qid=Q193292|lt=Heian period}} anthology ''[[:en:Songs to Make the Dust Dance on the Beams|Ryōjin Hishō]]'' associates the three shrines together, with Suwa Shrine being identified as the "head" of the three ''Nangū'' shrines (南宮の本山, ''nangu no honzan''), the shrine at Mino as the "midmost shrine" (中の宮, ''naka no miya''), and the shrine at Iga as the "youngest shrine" (稚の宮, ''chigo no miya'')''.''<ref>{{Cite book|last=Ōba|first=Yūsuke|title=竜神信仰: 諏訪神のルーツをさぐる (Ryujin shinkō: Suwa-gami no rūtsu o saguru)|publisher=Ronsōsha|year=2006|pages=137–138}}</ref>

''Hosshō'', meanwhile, is believed to refer to the concept of the ''{{ill|Dharmakāya|en|Dharmakāya|qid=Q1191427|lt=Dharmakāya}}'' (法性身, ''hosshōshin''), the formless, transcendent ultimate truth that is the source of all {{ill|Buddhahood|en|Buddhahood|qid=Q56247062|lt=buddhas}}, which are its physical manifestations (''{{ill|Nirmāṇakāya|en|Nirmāṇakāya|qid=Q3172811|lt=Nirmāṇakāya}}''). A certain medieval legend claims that the Suwa deity chose an eight-year-old boy to become his priest while declaring: "I have no (physical) body and so make this priest my [[Shintai|body]]".<ref name="miyasakayusho" /><ref>{{cite book |last1=Terada |first1=Shizuko |last2=Washio |first2=Tetsuta |title=諏訪明神―カミ信仰の原像 (Suwa Myōjin: Kami shinkō no genzō)|date=2010 |publisher=Iwata Shoin |page=116}}</ref>

==Mythology==

=== In imperial mythology ===

====Parentage====
Takeminakata is portrayed in both the ''Kojiki'' and the ''Sendai Kuji Hongi'' as a son of the god [[Ōkuninushi]], although the former does not include him in its genealogy of Ōkuninushi's children.<ref>Chamberlain (1882). [http://sacred-texts.com/shi/kj/kj033.htm Section XXVI.—The Deities the August Descendants of the Deity Master-of-the-Great-Land]</ref> The ''Kuji Hongi'' meanwhile identifies him as the son of Ōnamuchi (Ōkuninushi) with one of his wives, [[Nunakawahime]] of {{ill|Koshi Province (Japan)|en|Koshi Province (Japan)|qid=Q1351611|lt=Koshi}}.<ref name="Hongi" /><ref>Chamberlain (1882). [http://sacred-texts.com/shi/kj/kj031.htm Section XXIV.—The Wooing of the Deity-of-Eight-Thousand-Spears.]</ref>

====Defeat by Takemikazuchi====
{{see also|Kuni-yuzuri}}

[[File:Shinpukuji-bon Kojiki (真福寺本古事記).png|thumb|401x401px|The passage concerning Takeminakata's appearance and defeat from the oldest extant manuscript of the ''[[Kojiki]]'', the Shinpukuji-bon (真福寺本, written 1371–1372)]]Takeminakata appears in both the ''Kojiki'' and the ''Kuji Hongi'' in the context of Ōkuninushi's "transfer of the land" (''kuni-yuzuri'') to the ''[[amatsukami]]'', the gods of the heavenly realm of [[Takamagahara]].<ref name="Chamberlain" /><ref name="KujiHongi03">{{cite web|title=先代舊事本紀卷第三|url=http://miko.org/~uraki/kuon/furu/text/sendaikuji/sendaikuji03.htm|website=私本 先代舊事本紀}}</ref>

When the heavenly deities, headed by the sun goddess [[Amaterasu]] and/or the [[Kotoamatsukami|primordial deity]] [[Takamimusubi]], sent [[Takemikazuchi]] and another messenger{{efn|[[Kamiumi#Birth of the gods|Ame-no-Torifune]] in the ''Kojiki'', [[Futsunushi]] in the ''[[Nihon Shoki]]'' and the ''Kuji Hongi''}} to demand that Ōkuninushi relinquish his authority over the earthly realm of [[Ashihara no Nakatsukuni]] (the "Central Land of Reed-Plains") to Amaterasu's progeny, he told the messengers to consult his son [[Kotoshironushi-no-Mikoto|Kotoshironushi]], who immediately accepted their demands and advised his father to do likewise. Upon being asked if he had any other sons who ought to express their opinion, Ōkuninushi told the messengers that he had another son named Takeminakata.

<blockquote>As he was saying this, this same Takeminakata-no-Kami came bearing a tremendous boulder (千引之石, ''chibiki no iwa'', i.e. a boulder so large it would take a thousand men to pull) on his finger-tips and said:

"Who is it who has come to our land and is talking so furtively? Come, let us test our strength; I will first take your arm."

When [Takemikazuchi-no-Kami] allowed [Takeminakata-no-Kami] to take his arm, he changed it into a column of ice, then again changed it into a sword blade. At this, he (Takeminakata) was afraid and drew back.

Then [Takemikazuchi-no-Kami], in his turn, demanded [the right] to take hold of the arm of Takeminakata-no-Kami.

When he took it, it was like taking hold of a young reed; he grasped it and crushed it, throwing it aside. Immediately, he (Takeminakata) ran away.

They pursued him, and caught up with him by the {{ill|Lake Suwa|en|Lake Suwa|qid=Q1206692|lt=lake of Suwa}} in the {{ill|Shinano Province|en|Shinano Province|qid=Q289250|lt=land of Shinano}} (科野国州羽海). As they were about to kill him, Takeminakata-no-Kami said:

"Pray do not kill me. I will go to no other place. Also I will not disobey the commands of my father, Ōkuninushi-no-Kami, and will not disobey the words of the words of Yae-Kotoshironushi-no-Kami. I will yield this Central Land of the Reed Plains in accordance with the commands of the Heavenly Deities."<ref>Translation from {{cite book |last1=Philippi |first1=Donald L. |title=Kojiki |date=2015 |publisher=Princeton University Press |isbn=978-1400878000 |page=133 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=QzjWCgAAQBAJ&pg=PA133}} Names (transcribed in {{ill|Old Japanese|en|Old Japanese|qid=Q5736700|lt=Old Japanese}} in the original) have been changed into their modern equivalents.</ref></blockquote>

With Takeminakata's surrender, Ōkuninushi finally agreed to cede the land to the ''amatsukami'' and withdrew himself into the unseen spirit world.<ref name="Chamberlain" /><ref name="KujiHongi03" /><ref name="Hackin1932">{{cite book|author=J. Hackin|title=Asiatic Mythology: A Detailed Description and Explanation of the Mythologies of All the Great Nations of Asia|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=HAZrFhvqnTkC&pg=PA395|year=1932|publisher=Asian Educational Services|isbn=978-81-206-0920-4|page=395}}</ref><ref name="Herbert2010">{{cite book|author=Jean Herbert|title=Shinto: At the Fountainhead of Japan|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Sg_JBQAAQBAJ&pg=PT437|date=18 October 2010|publisher=Routledge|isbn=978-1-136-90376-2|page=437}}</ref><ref name="Ashkenazi2003">{{cite book|author=Michael Ashkenazi|title=Handbook of Japanese Mythology|url=https://archive.org/details/handbookofjapane0000ashk|url-access=registration|date=1 January 2003|publisher=ABC-CLIO|isbn=978-1-57607-467-1|pages=[https://archive.org/details/handbookofjapane0000ashk/page/267 267]–268}}</ref>

==== Variants and retellings ====

===== ''Suwa Daimyōjin Ekotoba'' =====
[[File:建御名方神 - Takeminakata.jpg|thumb|273x273px|Takeminakata carrying a heavy rock (''chibiki no iwa'') with his fingertips as a display of strength]]
The opening section of the ''{{ill|Suwa Daimyōjin Ekotoba|en|Suwa Daimyōjin Ekotoba|qid=Q11631818|lt=Suwa Daimyōjin Ekotoba}}'', a {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|en|Nanboku-chō period|qid=Q264012|lt=Nanboku-chō period}} compilation of legends and other information regarding Suwa Shrine and its festivals completed in 1356, retells the ''Kuji Hongi'' version of this story, albeit with Takeminakata's shameful defeat in the hands of Takemikazuchi notably omitted.<ref name="SuwaShishi685689">Suwa Shishi Hensan Iinkai, ed. (1995). pp. 685, 689.</ref>

<blockquote>It is said in the ''Kuji Hongi'' that Amaterasu-Ōmikami gave a decree and sent two gods, [[Futsunushi|Futsunushi-no-Kami]] (of [[Katori Jingū|Katori Shrine]] in {{ill|Shimōsa Province|en|Shimōsa Province|qid=Q1053695|lt=Shimōsa Province}}) and [[Takemikazuchi|Takeikatsuchi-no-Kami]] (of [[Kashima Jingū|Kashima Shrine]] in {{ill|Hitachi Province|en|Hitachi Province|qid=Q1055353|lt=Hitachi}}), down to the land of Izumo, where they declared to [[Ōkuninushi|Ōanamuchi]] (of [[Izumo-taisha|Kitsuki]] in {{ill|Izumo Province|en|Izumo Province|qid=Q582846|lt=Izumo}} [and] {{ill|Ōmiwa Shrine|en|Ōmiwa Shrine|qid=Q705542|lt=Miwa}} in {{ill|Yamato Province|en|Yamato Province|qid=Q907495|lt=Yamato}}), "The Central Land of Reed-Plains is the land entrusted to our heir. Are you willing to give it up to the heavenly deities?"
Ōanamuchi said, "Ask my son, [[Kotoshironushi-no-Mikoto|Kotoshironushi-no-Kami]] (of [[Nagata Shrine]] in {{ill|Settsu Province|en|Settsu Province|qid=Q864163|lt=Settsu}}; eighth [patron deity of] the [[Department of Divinities|Jingi-kan]]); he will give you an answer."<br />Kotoshironushi-no-Kami said, "My father ought respectfully to withdraw, nor will I disobey."<br />[The messengers said,] "Do you have any other sons who ought to speak?"<br />"There is also my son, Takeminakata-no-Kami (of Suwa Shrine)."<br />[He] came, bearing a heavy boulder on his fingertips, saying, "Who is it who has come to our land and is talking so furtively? I wish to challenge you to a test of strength."

When he took his hand, <em>he caused ice to appear, and then he manifested a sword</em>. Upon arriving at the sea of Suwa in the land of Shinano, Takeminakata-no-Kami said, "I will go to no other place."

This is the {{ill|Pratītyasamutpāda|en|Pratītyasamutpāda|qid=Q522046|lt=karmic origins}} of the [Suwa deity's] [[Honji suijaku|manifest trace]] (垂迹の本縁, ''suijaku no hon'en'').{{efn|「天照太神ミコトノリシテ経津主ノ<small>総州香取社</small>神武甕槌ノ<small>常州鹿島社</small>神二柱ノ神ヲIzumo Province ニ降タテマツリテ、大己貴<small>雲州杵築・和州三輪</small>ノ命ニ問テノタマハク、葦原ノ中津国者我御子の知ラスヘキ国ナリ。汝マサニ此国ヲモテ天ノ神ニ奉ンヤ、大己貴ノ命申サク、我子事代主<small>摂州長田社・神祇官第八</small>ノ神ニ問テ返事申サント申、事代主神申サク、我父ヨロシクマサニサリ奉ルヘシ。ワレモ我タカウヘカラスト申。又申ヘキ子アリヤ、又我子建御名方<small>諏訪社</small>ノ神、千引ノ石ヲ手末ニサヽケテ来テ申サク、是我国ニキタリテ、シノヒテカクイフハ、シカウシテ力クラヘセント思、先ソノ御手ヲ取テ即氷ヲ成立、又剣ヲ取成、科野ノ国洲羽ノ海ニイタルトキ、当御名方ノ神申サク、ワレ此国ヲ除者他処ニ不行云々、是則当社垂迹ノ本縁也。」<ref>''Suwa Daimyōjin Ekotoba'', in Kanai (1982). p. 219.</ref>}}<ref>Yamashita (2006). p. 9.</ref></blockquote>

Although it was formerly thought that the ''Ekotoba''<nowiki/>'s compiler, [[:ja:諏訪円忠|Suwa (Kosaka) Enchū]] (1295-1364, a member of a cadet branch of the Suwa clan based in {{ill|Kyoto|en|Kyoto|qid=Q34600|lt=Kyoto}}) was responsible for excising Takeminakata's defeat out of this retelling in order to portray the deity in a more positive light, <ref name="SuwaShishi685689" /> Ryōtarō Maeda (2020) put forward the alternative explanation that Enchū may have made use from an anthology of excerpts or ''{{ill|Florilegium|en|Florilegium|qid=Q354326|lt=Florilegium}}'' that happened to omit the relevant passage. He identifies Enchū's source text with an extract of the ''Kuji Hongi'' ''kuni-yuzuri'' narrative titled "The Matter of Suwa Shrine" (諏方社事, ''Suwa-sha no koto''), which was in turn appended to a lengthy extract of the ''Kojiki''<nowiki/>'s ''kuni-yuzuri'' account (古事記上巻抄, ''Kojiki Jōkan-shō'', "Excerpt from the Upper Volume of the ''Kojiki''") found in the temple library of Shinpuku-ji ({{ill|Ōsu Kannon|en|Ōsu Kannon|qid=Q3594052|lt=Ōsu Kannon}}) in {{ill|Nagoya|en|Nagoya|qid=Q11751|lt=Nagoya}}.<ref name="Kojikijokan">{{Cite web |title=古事記上巻抄 (Kojiki Jо̄kan-shо̄) |url=https://dl.ndl.go.jp/pid/3438605 |access-date=2023-08-15 |website=NDL Digital Collections |publisher=Koten Hozon-kai (古典保存会) |publication-date=1924}}</ref><ref name=":0">Maeda (2020). pp. 43–57.</ref>

{{Blockquote
|text="(...) When he allowed him to take his hand, he changed it into a column of ice, and then changed it into a sword blade," <em>{{ill|Et cetera|en|Et cetera|qid=Q845653|lt=and so forth}}</em> (, ''unnun'').<br/>
"Upon arriving at the sea of Suwa in the land of Shinano, Takeminakata-no-Kami said, 'I will go to no other place. And I will not disobey the commands of my father Ōkuninushi-no-Kami, and will not disobey the words of the words of my elder brother Yae-Kotoshironushi-no-Kami. I will yield this Central Land of the Reed Plains in accordance with the commands of the Heavenly Deities.'"|source="The Matter of Suwa Shrine" (諏方社事, ''Suwa-sha no koto'')<ref name="Kojikijokan" /><ref name=":0" />}}

[[File:諏方社事 - Suwa-sha no Koto.png|left|thumb|Part of "The Matter of Suwa Shrine" (諏方社事, ''Suwa-sha no koto'') appended to the {{ill|Ōsu Kannon|en|Ōsu Kannon|qid=Q3594052|lt=Shinpuku-ji}} ''Kojiki Jōkan-shō''. The omission of the passage recounting Takeminakata's defeat is marked with an  (''unnun'', "and so forth," "etc." - fourth column from left)]]
Based on textual affinities with the Urabe text of the ''Kojiki'', the ''Jōkan-shō'' is thought to have been authored by a member of the priestly [[Japanese clans#Sacerdotal clans|Urabe clan]] associated with the {{ill|Yoshida Shrine|en|Yoshida Shrine|qid=Q713177|lt=Yoshida}} and [[Hirano Shrine|Hirano Shrines]] in Kyoto. Records indicate that during the medieval period, the ''Kuji Hongi'' was used by the [[Department of Divinities]] or ''Jingi-kan'' (in which many Urabe clan members occupied posts) as a go-to source for inquiries regarding the histories of various shrines across the country. It is also known that during his research for information regarding Suwa Shrine, Enchū sought the assistance of two Urabe clan members: Urabe Kanetoyo (卜部兼豊, of the Yoshida branch), then senior assistant director (神祇大輔, ''jingi taifu'') of the Jingi-kan, and Urabe Kanemae (卜部兼前, of the Hirano branch), either of whom may have been responsible for compiling "The Matter of Suwa Shrine." In other words, Enchu most likely did not (or could not) consult the ''Kuji Hongi'' itself, but was rather working with an extract provided by his Urabe contacts.<ref name=":0" />
[[File:Izumo okinoshima.jpg|thumb|Inasa Beach in {{ill|Izumo|en|Izumo|qid=Q301580|lt=Izumo}}, {{ill|Shimane Prefecture|en|Shimane Prefecture|qid=Q132751|lt=Shimane Prefecture}}, the setting of the ''kuni-yuzuri'' myth cycle]]
Although he was not responsible for excising Takeminakata's surrender from the narrative himself, its absence from his source allowed Enchū to reimagine the ''Kuji Hongi'' narrative in a way that portrayed Takeminakata as a triumphant god who vowed to remain in Suwa of his own volition, consistent with the portrayal of the god of Suwa as an illustrious warrior deity in the ''Ekotoba''<nowiki/>'s later portions. Whereas in the original ''Kojiki'' and ''Kuji Hongi'' narrative, Takemikazuchi is said to have "changed [his arm] into a column of ice, then again changed it into a sword blade" (取成立氷亦取成劍刃) after having it grasped by Takeminakata, Enchū - taking advantage of the ambiguous syntax of the original {{ill|Classical Chinese|en|Classical Chinese|qid=Q37041|lt=Classical Chinese}} text - chooses to read the text such that ''Takeminakata'' is now said to magically materialize ice and a sword as a display of his power to Takemikazuchi (即氷ヲ成立、又劍ヲ取成, "he (Takeminakata) caused ice to appear, and then he manifested a sword").<ref name=":0" />

Before (and to an extent, even after) the rediscovery and subsequent boom in popularity of the ''Kojiki'' in the middle of the {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|qid=Q184963|lt=Edo period}}, the more positive image of Takeminakata as presented in the ''Suwa Daimyōjin Ekotoba'' exerted considerable influence in the way the ''kuni-yuzuri'' myth is recounted in {{ill|Early modern period|en|Early modern period|qid=Q5308718|lt=early modern}} documents associated with Suwa Shrine, not least because it apparently introduced the myth (which seems to have originally been specific to the imperial court - see '[[Takeminakata#Analysis|Analysis]]' below) into Suwa itself - where other myths concerning the Suwa deity were in circulation - for the first time.<ref name="Maeda2023">Maeda (2023). pp. 16-30.</ref>

Ryōtarō Maeda (2023), based on a study of surviving manuscripts of the text, postulates that the ''Ekotoba'' was only introduced to Suwa itself no earlier than the 17th century, where it gradually gained acceptance among the priestly families of Suwa Shrine, who produced a number of copies of it. Soon, the influence of the ''Ekotoba'' can be seen in a number of texts from the area: a text penned by the ''{{ill|Hatamoto|en|Hatamoto|qid=Q572662|lt=Hatamoto}}'' [[:ja:諏訪盛條|Suwa Morieda]] (1646-1695), the younger brother of [[Suwa Domain#Suwa Tadaharu|Suwa Tadaharu]], the third ''daimyō'' of {{ill|Suwa Domain|en|Suwa Domain|qid=Q3034531|lt=Takashima Domain}} in 1684 titled ''Shinshu Suwa Daimyōjin Engi'' (信州諏方大明神縁起, "The Origin Story of Suwa Daimyōjin of Shinano Province"), for instance, features the reinterpreted ''kuni-yuzuri'' myth, which Morieda then interprets in a {{ill|Edo neo-Confucianism|en|Edo neo-Confucianism|qid=Q5340141|lt=Neo-Confucian}} light as a meritorious act of filial piety comparable to {{ill|Taibo|en|Taibo|qid=Q1010535|lt=Taibo}}'s renunciation of the throne of {{ill|Predynastic Zhou|en|Predynastic Zhou|qid=Q16924982|lt=Zhou}}.<ref name="Maeda2023"/>

{{Blockquote
|text=They (Futsunushi and Takemikazuchi) also made the declaration [to cede the land] to this god (Takeminakata), but this god would not easily give his assent. Bearing a heavy boulder on his fingertips, he came, saying, "Who has come forth, saying these things? I wish to have a contest of strength." [But] he repented and eventually ceded the Central Land to the Heavenly Grandson. He departed, arriving at the sea of Suwa in the land of Shinano.<br/>
'It may be said that he is supreme in virtue, and the people could not praise him [enough].' (可謂至徳也、已民無得而稱焉){{efn|Quotation from {{ill|Confucius|en|Confucius|qid=Q4604|lt=Confucius}}' ''{{ill|Analects|en|Analects|qid=Q276015|lt=Analects}}'': "It may be said that Taibo was supreme in virtue. Three times he renounced the sovereignty of {{ill|Tianxia|en|Tianxia|qid=Q955223|lt=all things under Heaven}}, but the people could not praise him." (泰伯其可謂至徳也已矣、三以天下譲、民無得而稱焉。)}} This is he who is now known as Suwa Daimyōjin.<ref>Maeda (2023). pp. 21-23.</ref>}}

[[File:Lake Suwa 20131231 - panoramio (cropped).jpg|thumb|{{ill|Lake Suwa|en|Lake Suwa|qid=Q1206692|lt=Lake Suwa}}]]
As late as the 19th century (when awareness of the ''Kojiki''<nowiki/>'s contents had become much more widespread due to the efforts of ''{{ill|Kokugaku|en|Kokugaku|qid=Q855159|lt=Kokugaku}}'' scholars), this positive reinterpretation of the ''kuni-yuzuri'' narrative continued to be found within Suwa: a mid-19th century genealogical chart of Takeminakata issued by the Upper Shrine for instance quotes the above passage from the ''Shinshu Suwa Daimyōjin Engi''.<ref>Maeda (2023). p. 23.</ref> A document submitted in 1834 to the Commissioner of Shrines and Temples (''[[Jisha-bugyō]]'') by the Lower Shrine's Momoi clan (桃井氏) of priests relates the following:

{{Blockquote
|text=When the two deities of Kashima and Katori came down to the land of Izumo at the command of the heavenly deities, he [Takeminakata] fought for his land bearing a heavy rock on his fingertips and engaged in a test of strength. <em>He also took up a sword and exhibited valor.</em> When he, leading [an army of] divine soldiers, arrived at the sea of Suwa in the land of Shinano, he offered up the Central Land of the Reed Plains to the Heavenly Grandson. As his divine father had ceded the land, he made a vow to never go to another place. This is the account of this shrine's establishment.<ref>Maeda (2023). p. 24.</ref>}}

A third text found in the archives of the Upper Shrine's Moriya (守矢氏) priestly clan titled "The Origin of Suwa Daimyōjin" (諏訪大明神由来, ''Suwa Daimyōjin yurai'') features Takeminakata striking fear into Futsunushi and Takemikazuchi after displaying his power to them, only agreeing to cede Ashihara no Nakatsukuni after he was convinced by their reasoning. The three then go to Suwa, where they defeat the local deity [[Moriya|Moriya]] (see below).<ref>Maeda (2023). p. 30.</ref>

===== Other versions =====
Similar attempts at retelling or reinterpreting the myth in a more positive way are found in other texts. In one version, for instance, Takeminakata is portrayed as going to Suwa not so much to flee from Takemikazuchi but to pacify it under the orders of his father Ōkuninushi.<ref>Miyaji (1937). pp. 48-49.</ref>

A variant found in a commentary on the ''Nihon Shoki'' penned by a 15th-century monk named Shun'yu (春瑜), the ''Nihon Shoki Shikenmon'' (日本書紀私見聞), claims 'Suwa Daimyōjin' (諏防大明神) to be the third son of the deity [[:ja:山王権現|Sannō Gongen]], the guardian deity of {{ill|Mount Hiei|en|Mount Hiei|qid=Q748040|lt=Mount Hiei}}. After engaging in a failed rebellion against Amaterasu, the deity surrendered and settled down in the land of Shinano.<ref>Miyaji (1937). pp. 47.</ref>

Local legends from within Nagano Prefecture claim Takeminakata to have passed or stayed in various places within the region during his escape. A local legend in {{ill|Shimoina District, Nagano|en|Shimoina District, Nagano|qid=Q726999|lt=Shimoina District}} (located south of Suwa) for instance claims that Takemikazuchi caught up with the fleeing Takeminakata in the modern village of {{ill|Toyooka, Nagano|en|Toyooka, Nagano|qid=Q44545|lt=Toyooka}}, where they agreed to an armistice and left imprints of their hands on a rock as a sign of their agreement. The rock, bearing the gods' supposed handprints (''tegata''), is found in Otegata Shrine (御手形神社) in Toyooka.<ref>{{cite web |title=国護りと天孫降臨の神話ー御手形石ー |url=http://www.ja-mis.iijan.or.jp/gotominami/hometown/2016/11/post_140.php |website=JA Minami Shinshu official website}}</ref> After Takemikazuchi's departure, Takeminakata temporarily resided in the neighboring village of {{ill|Ōshika, Nagano|en|Ōshika, Nagano|qid=Q1203751|lt=Ōshika}}, where he discovered hot springs of saltwater while hunting for deer.<ref>{{cite web |title=塩水の湧泉から採取される大鹿村の山塩の謎 |url=http://www.iijan.or.jp/oishii/area/post-1085.php |website=長野県のおいしい食べ方 |date=June 23, 2009 |publisher=JA Nagano Chuoukai}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Matsumae |first1=Takashi |title=日本神話の形成 (Nihon shinwa no keisei) |publisher=Hanawa Shobō|page=431}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |editor1-last=Satō|editor1-first=Shigenao|title=南信伊那史料 巻之下 (Nanshin Ina Shiryō, vol. 02)|date=1901|page=55 |url=http://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/765237/30}}</ref>

The contest between Takemikazuchi and Takeminakata has also been sometimes interpreted as an {{ill|Origin myth|en|Origin myth|qid=Q390248|lt=Origin myth}} for {{ill|Sumo|en|Sumo|qid=Q40561|lt=sumo wrestling}} and {{ill|Aiki (martial arts principle)|en|Aiki (martial arts principle)|qid=Q3305458|lt=aiki}}.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Pate|first1=Alan Scott|title=Ningyo: The Art of the Japanese Doll|date=2013|publisher=Tuttle Publishing|isbn=978-1462907205|pages=135–136|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=EzzRAgAAQBAJ&pg=PT136}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|editor1-last=Spracklen|editor1-first=Karl|editor2-last=Lashua|editor2-first=Brett|editor3-last=Sharpe|editor3-first=Erin|editor4-last=Swain|editor4-first=Spencer|title=The Palgrave Handbook of Leisure Theory|date=2017|publisher=978-1137564795|pages=173–175|isbn=9781137564795 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=7_2yDgAAQBAJ&pg=PA173}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Von Krenner |first1=Walther G. |last2=Apodaca |first2=Damon |last3=Jeremiah |first3=Ken |title=Aikido Ground Fighting: Grappling and Submission Techniques |date=2013 |publisher=North Atlantic Books |isbn=978-1583946213 |pages=6–7 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=fGynTN3nQC4C&pg=PA7}}</ref> This interpretation apparently follows an alternative reading of the text which sees Takemikazuchi as not so much crushing and tearing Takeminakata's arm(s) off but seizing him by the arm and throwing him into the ground.

=== Other myths ===

====Entry into Suwa====
{{see also|Moreya}}

[[File:Fujishima Shrine (Nakasu, Suwa) - 藤島社（諏訪市中洲）- 2.jpg|thumb|353x353px|Fujishima Shrine (藤島社) in [[:en:Suwa City|Suwa City]]. It is one of two 'Fujishima Shrines' associated with Suwa Myōjin's battle against Moriya; the other is located in {{ill|Okaya, Nagano|en|Okaya, Nagano|qid=Q838672|lt=the city of Okaya}} by the Tenryū River.]]
A myth from the Suwa area portrays Suwa Myōjin as being opposed during his advent by the local god [[Moriya|Moriya]] (Moreya).

A document supposedly submitted to the {{ill|Kamakura shogunate|en|Kamakura shogunate|qid=Q736839|lt=Kamakura shogunate}} in 1249 by Suwa Nobushige, then high priest or ''Ōhōri'' (大祝) of the Upper Shrine of Suwa, known as the ''Suwa Nobushige Gejō'' (諏訪信重解状 "The Petition of Suwa Nobushige"), relates a story from "the ancient customs" (舊貫) that the Suwa deity came down from heaven in order to take possession of the land of 'Moriya Daijin' (守屋大臣). The conflict between the two escalated into a battle, but as no winner could be declared, the two finally compete in a {{ill|Tug of war|en|Tug of war|qid=Q102843|lt=Tug of war}} using hooks (''kagi''): Suwa Myōjin, using a hook made out of the [[wisteria]] plant (藤鎰), emerges victorious against Moriya, who used an iron hook (鐵鎰). After his victory, the god built his dwelling (what would become the Upper Shrine) in Moriya's land and planted the wisteria hook, which became a grove known as the 'Forest of Fujisuwa' (藤諏訪之森 ''Fujisuwa no mori'').{{efn|「一 守屋山麓御垂跡事<br>
右謹檢舊貫、當砌昔者守屋大臣之所領也、大神天降御之刻、大臣者奉禦明神之居住、勵制止之方法、明神者廻可爲御敷地之祕計、或致諍論、或及合戰之處、兩方難決雌雄、爰明神者持藤鎰、大臣者以鐵鎰、懸此所引之、明神即以藤鎰令勝得軍陣之諍論給、而間令追罰守屋大臣、卜居所當社以來、遙送數百歲星霜、久施我神之稱譽天下給、應跡之方々是新哉、明神以彼藤鎰自令植當社之前給、藤榮枝葉號藤諏訪之森、毎年二ヶ度御神事勤之、自尓以來以當郡名諏方、爰下宮者當社依夫婦之契約示姫大明神之名、然而當大明神、若不令追出守屋給者、爭兩者卜居御哉、自天降之元初爲本宮之條炳焉者哉、」}}<ref name="GejoEkotoba">Suwa Shishi Hensan Iinkai, ed. (1995). pp. 811–814.</ref><ref name="Miyasaka9293">Miyasaka (1992). pp. 92-93.</ref><ref name="fukudachusei">Fukuda; Nihonmatsu; Tokuda, eds. (2015). pp. 121-124.</ref> Whereas the ''Kojiki'' portrays Takeminakata as an earthly god defeated by a deity from heaven, this myth notably features the opposite scenario, in which the deity of Suwa descends from heaven and conquers the land below.

The ''Suwa Daimyōjin Ekotoba'' relates a variant of this myth as an origin story of Fujishima Shrine (藤島社) in {{ill|Suwa, Nagano|en|Suwa, Nagano|qid=Q846338|lt=Suwa City}}, one of the Upper Shrine's [[Setsumatsusha|auxiliary shrines]] where its yearly rice-planting ceremony is traditionally held.<ref name="fukudachusei"/><ref name="Suwashishi681">Suwa Shishi Hensan Iinkai, ed. (1995). pp. 681-683.</ref><ref>Miyasaka (1992). pp. 88-91.</ref> In this version, the deity of Fujishima Shrine (藤島の明神 ''Fujishima no Myōjin'') - usually equated with Suwa Myōjin - defeats "Moriya the evil outlaw" (洩矢の惡賊, ''Moriya no akuzoku'') with a wisteria branch:

{{Quote|Regarding the god of Fujishima [Shrine] (藤島の明神, ''Fujishima no Myōjin''): when the revered deity (尊神, ''sonjin'', i.e. Suwa Daimyōjin) [[Honji suijaku|manifested]] long ago, Moriya the evil outlaw (洩矢の惡賊, ''Moriya no akuzoku''), seeking to hinder him, took up an iron ring (鐵輪) to fight him, but the [Fujishima] deity picked up a wisteria branch and defeated [Moriya]. Finally, he brought down heresy (邪輪, ''jarin'', lit. "ring/wheel/circle of evil") and held up {{ill|Dharma (Buddhism)|en|Dharma (Buddhism)|qid=Q9241518|lt=the true Dharma}} (正法, ''shōbō''). When the god pronounced a vow and threw the wisteria branch away, immediately it took root [in the ground], its branches and leaves flourishing in abundance, and [sprouted] beautiful blossoms, leaving behind a marker of the battleground for posterity. The Fujishima deity is named thus for this reason.{{efn|「抑コノ藤嶋ノ明神ト申ハ、尊神垂迹ノ昔、洩矢ノ惡賊神居ヲサマタケントセシ時、洩矢ハ鐵輪ヲ持シテアラソヒ、明神ハ藤枝ヲトリテ是ヲ伏シ給フ。ツイニ邪輪ヲ降シテ正法ヲ興ス。 明神誓ヲ發テ、藤枝ヲナケ給シカハ、則根ヲサシテ枝葉ヲサカヘ、花蘂アサヤカニシテ、戰場ノシルシヲ萬代ニ殘ス。藤嶋ノ明神ト号スル此ユヘナリ。」}}<ref>Kanai (1982). p. 262.</ref><ref>Hanawa, ed. (1914). p. 530.</ref>}}
[[File:Fujishima Shrine - 藤島神社 (川岸天竜河畔諏訪明神入諏伝説の地).jpg|alt=|thumb|Fujishima Shrine (藤島神社) in {{ill|Okaya, Nagano|en|Okaya, Nagano|qid=Q838672|lt=Okaya}}]]
Two extant medieval genealogies of the Suwa (Miwa) clan also begin by recounting the legend of a battle between the Suwa deity, accompanied by the first high priest of the Upper Shrine, and 'Moriya' (守屋) during the reign of {{ill|Emperor Yōmei|en|Emperor Yōmei|qid=Q349281|lt=Emperor Yōmei}} (585-587).<ref>Suwa Shishi Hensan Iinkai, ed. (1995). p. 690.</ref>

In later versions of this story which combine it with the ''kuni-yuzuri'' myth, Moriya opposes Takeminakata after the latter had fled from Izumo. After being defeated, Moriya swears fealty to Takeminakata and becomes a faithful ally.<ref name="Imai1960">Imai (1960). pp. 3-15.</ref><ref name="Imai1976">Imai (1976). p. 41.</ref> Moriya is reckoned as the divine ancestor of the Moriya (守矢) clan, one of the former priestly lineages of the Upper Shrine.<ref name="Moriya">Moriya, Sanae (2017). ''守矢神長家のお話し (Moriya Jinchōke no ohanashi),'' in {{cite book |editor=Jinchōkan Moriya Historical Museum |title=神長官守矢史料館のしおり (Jinchōkan Moriya Shiryōkan no shiori)|pages=2–3|publisher=Jinchōkan Moriya Historical Museum|edition=3rd}}</ref>

While medieval sources such as Nobushige's petition and the ''Ekotoba'' situate the battle between the two gods in the slopes of [[Mount Moriya|Mount Moriya]] somewhere in the vicinity of the Upper Shrine (modern {{ill|Suwa, Nagano|en|Suwa, Nagano|qid=Q846338|lt=Suwa City}}), a variant legend first attested in {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|qid=Q184963|lt=Edo period}} texts instead place it on the banks of the [[Tenryū River]] (modern {{ill|Okaya, Nagano|en|Okaya, Nagano|qid=Q838672|lt=Okaya City}}).<ref name="yamamoto">{{cite journal |author=Yamamoto, Hiroko|title=中世諏訪社の一考察 : 失われた芸能と伝承を求めて (''Chūsei Suwa-sha no ikkōsatsu: ushinawareta geinō to denshō o motomete'')|journal=Tozai Nanboku: Bulletin of the Wako Institute of Social and Cultural Sciences|year=2016|pages=[29–31] 215–213|url=https://wako.repo.nii.ac.jp/?action=repository_uri&item_id=4029&file_id=22&file_no=1}}</ref><ref name="Imai1960" /><ref name="Moriya" /><ref>{{cite web |title=洩矢神社 (Moriya Shrine) |url=http://www.nagano-jinjacho.jp/shibu/04nansin/02suwa/4030.html |website=長野県神社庁 (Nagano-ken Jinjachō)}}</ref>

[[File:Tatsuya-Sukura Shrine , 達屋酢蔵神社 - panoramio (1).jpg|left|thumb|Tatsuya-Sukura Shrine (達屋酢蔵神社) in {{ill|Chino, Nagano|en|Chino, Nagano|qid=Q838660|lt=Chino}}, associated with the gods Yatsukao (Ganigawara) and Hikosachi in folklore]]

Apart from Moriya, a few scattered local legends make reference to other deities who either submitted to the Suwa deity or refused to do so. One such god that is said to have opposed Suwa Myōjin and his new ally Moriya in local folklore was Yatsukao-no-Mikoto (矢塚男命), also known as Ganigawara (蟹河原長者 ''Ganigawara-chōja'').<ref name="Kobuzoku79">Kobuzoku Kenkyūkai, ed. (2017b). p 79.</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=蟹河原 （茅野市ちの横内）|url=http://tateshina-times.jp/?p=7866|website=たてしなの時間|publisher=蓼科企画}}</ref><ref name="suwashi-keizu">''Shinano-no-kuni Kansha Suwa-jinja Jinchōkan Moriya-ke Ryaku-keizu'' (信濃國官社諏訪神社神長官守矢家略系圖), in {{cite book|author1=Nobukawa, Kazuhiko (延川和彦)|author2=Iida, Kotaro (飯田好太郎)|title=諏訪氏系図 続編 (Suwa-shi Keizu, Zokuhen)|date=1921|page=19|url=http://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/927368/21}}</ref>

The story relates that Ganigawara, a horse breeder who wielded great authority in the region, held Moriya in contempt for surrendering to Takeminakata and had messengers publicly harass him by calling him a coward. When Ganigawara's servants began to resort to violence by shooting arrows in Takeminakata's newly built house, Takeminakata retaliated by invading Ganigawara's turf. Mortally wounded by an arrow in the ensuing battle, Ganigawara begs forgiveness from Moriya and entrusts his youngest daughter to Takeminakata, who gives her in marriage to the god Taokihooi-no-Mikoto (手置帆負命) a.k.a. Hikosachi-no-Kami (彦狭知神),{{efn|Both Taokihooi and Hikosachi - identified as two distinct individuals - appear in the ''[[Nihon Shoki]]''<ref>{{cite wikisource |title=Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697 |wslink=Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697 |chapter=Book II |last=Aston |first=William George |authorlink=William George Aston |year=1896 |publisher=Kegan Paul, Trench, Trübner & Co. |location=London |page=81 |scan=Page:Nihongi_by_Aston.djvu/112 |quote=Thereupon Ta-oki-ho-ohi no Kami, ancestor of the Imbe of the Land of Kii, was appointed hatter, Hiko-sachi no Kami was made shield-maker ...}}</ref><ref>{{cite wikisource |wslink=zh:日本書紀 |chapter=卷第二 |title=日本書紀 |quote=既以紀伊國忌部遠祖手置帆負神、定爲作笠者。狹知神、爲作盾者。}}</ref> and the ''[[Kogo Shūi]]''<ref>{{cite wikisource |wslink=zh:古語拾遺 |title=古語拾遺 |quote=手置帆負命。<sub>讚岐國忌部祖也。</sub>產狹知命。<sub>紀伊國忌部祖也。</sub>}}</ref> as ancestors of the Inbe clan (忌部氏).}} who was injured by Ganigawara's messengers as he was keeping watch over Takeminakata's abode.<ref>Imai (1960). pp. 42-49.</ref><ref>Imai (1976). pp. 46-51.</ref>

In another legend, a god named Takei-Ōtomonushi (武居大伴主神 or 武居大友主神) swore allegiance to Takeminakata and became the ancestor of a line of priests in the Lower Shrine known as the ''Takeihōri'' (武居祝).<ref>Miyasaka (1987). p. 22.</ref><ref name="Kobuzoku79" /> Yet another story relates that the Suwa deity forbade the goddess of Sakinomiya Shrine (先宮神社) in Owa, {{ill|Suwa, Nagano|en|Suwa, Nagano|qid=Q846338|lt=Suwa City}} from building a bridge over the creek before her shrine as punishment for her refusal to submit to him.<ref name="Kobuzoku79" /><ref>{{cite web |title=先宮神社 |url=https://www.jinriki.info/kaidolist/koshukaido/kamisuwa_shimosuwa/sakinomiyajinja.html |website=人力（じんりき）- 旧街道ウォーキング}}</ref>

====The ''Ōhōri''====
{{see also|Suwa clan}}

[[File:Japanese crest Suwa Kajinoha(White background).svg|thumb|left|The crest (''[[:en:Kamon (crest)|kamon]]'') of the [[Suwa clan]], which is also used by the Upper Shrine of Suwa as its emblem.]]
Before the abolition of the Suwa Grand Shrine's traditional priestly offices during the {{ill|Meiji era|en|Meiji era|qid=Q3125096|lt=Meiji era}}, the Upper Shrine of Suwa's high priest or ''Ōhōri'' (大祝  'great priest'; also ''Ōhafuri'') was a young boy chosen from the [[Suwa clan]], who was, during his term of office, considered to be [[Arahitogami|a living god]], the visible incarnation or 'body' of the unseen god of the shrine.<ref name="Ihara">Ihara (2008). pp. 157–185.</ref><ref>{{cite book|date=1988|editor1-last=Hall|editor1-first=John Whitney|title=The Cambridge History of Japan, Volume 1: Ancient Japan|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-0521223522|page=343|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=A3_6lp8IOK8C&pg=PA343}}</ref>

The legend of how Suwa Myōjin chose his first priest is recounted in various sources, such as the ''Suwa Daimyōjin Ekotoba'':

<blockquote>At the beginning of the god's [[Honji suijaku|manifestation]], he took off his robe, put them on an eight year old boy, and dubbed him 'great priest' (''Ōhōri''). The god declared, "I do not have a body and so make this priest (''hōri'') my body."<br />
This [boy] is Arikazu (有員), the priest of the sacred robe (御衣祝 ''Misogihōri''), the founding ancestor of the Miwa/Jin (神, i.e. Suwa) clan.{{efn|「祝は神明の垂迹の初。御衣を八歳の童男にぬぎきせ給ひて。大祝と称し。我において体なし。祝を以て躰とすと神勅ありけり。是則御衣祝有員神氏の始祖なり。」<ref name="EkotobaHori">''Suwa Daimyōjin Ekotoba'', in Hanawa (1919). pp. 521–522.</ref>}}</blockquote>

[[File:Suwa Daimyōjin - 諏訪大明神.jpg|thumb|200px|Suwa Myōjin as a warrior in hunting gear]]
Although most sources (such as the ''Ekotoba'' above) identify the boy with the semi-legendary priest Arikazu, who is said to have lived in the {{ill|9th century|en|9th century|qid=Q8083|lt=9th century}} (early {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|qid=Q193292|lt=Heian period}}) during the reign of [[Emperor Kanmu]] (781-806) or his immediate successors {{ill|Emperor Heizei|en|Emperor Heizei|qid=Q353558|lt=Heizei}} (806-809) or {{ill|Emperor Saga|en|Emperor Saga|qid=Q316654|lt=Saga}} (809-823),<ref name="Shinenpyo">Suwa Kyōikukai (1938). p. 11.{{in lang|ja}}</ref><ref name="Miyasaka35">Miyasaka (1987). p. 35.</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=大祝有員 (Ōhōri Arikazu)|url=http://www.city.suwa.lg.jp/scm/dat/nandemo/koumoku/0300/030504.htm|website=Official website of Suwa City {{in lang|ja}}|access-date=May 14, 2017|archive-date=September 8, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170908112038/http://www.city.suwa.lg.jp/scm/dat/nandemo/koumoku/0300/030504.htm|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=諏方氏 (Suwa Clan)|url=http://www.city.suwa.lg.jp/scm/dat/nandemo/koumoku/0300/030503.htm|website=Official website of Suwa City {{in lang|ja}}|access-date=February 16, 2017|archive-date=February 8, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170208132946/http://www.city.suwa.lg.jp/scm/dat/nandemo/koumoku/0300/030503.htm|url-status=dead}}</ref> two genealogical lists - of disputed historical reliability<ref>Ihara (2008). pp. 260-262.</ref><ref>{{cite web|author=Fukushima, Masaki|title=信濃古代の通史叙述をめぐって (Shinano kodai no tsūshi jojutsu wo megutte)|url=http://user1.matsumoto.ne.jp/~fukusima/yamakawa.htm|website=科野太郎の古代・中世史の部屋|access-date=2017-09-24|archive-date=October 19, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211019150040/http://user1.matsumoto.ne.jp/~fukusima/yamakawa.htm|url-status=dead}}</ref> - instead identify the first priest with an individual named Otoei (乙頴) or Kumako (神子 or 熊古), a son of Mase-gimi (麻背君) or Iotari (五百足), head of the Kanasashi clan and ''[[kuni no miyatsuko]]'' of Shinano during the late 6th century.<ref>Miyasaka (1987). pp. 35-36.</ref><ref>Miyasaka (1992), pp. 7–11.</ref>

One of these two texts is a genealogy of the Aso (阿蘇) clan of [[Aso Shrine]] in [[Kyushu]] known as the 異本阿蘇氏系図 (''Ihon Asoshi Keizu'').<ref>Kanai, Tenbi (2018). 諏訪信仰の性格とその変遷―諏訪信仰通史 (''Suwa shinkō no seikaku to sono hensen: Suwa shinko tsūshi''). in Kodai Buzoku Kenkyūkai, ed. pp. 36-38.</ref><ref name="Asoshi">''Ihon Asoshi Keizu'', cited in Kanai (1982). p. 109.</ref> It reads in part:

<blockquote>Otoei (''Ōhōri'' of the great god of Suwa): also known as Kumako (神子) or Kumako (熊古).<br />
When he was eight years old, the great god Minakatatomi-no-Mikoto appeared, took off his robe and put them on Kumako, declaring, "I do not have a body and so make you my body." In the third month of the second year of {{ill|Emperor Yōmei|en|Emperor Yōmei|qid=Q349281|lt=Iware Ikebe no Ōmiya}} (587), a sanctuary (社壇) was built at the foot of the mountain at the southern side of the lake (i.e. Lake Suwa) to worship the great god of Suwa and various other gods ...{{efn|「乙頴 (諏訪大神大祝)：一名神子、又云、熊古　生而八歳、御名方富命大神化現脱着御衣於神子勅曰、吾無体以汝為体、盤余池辺大宮朝二年丁未三月搆壇于湖南山麓、祭諏訪大明神及百八十神、奉千代田刺忌串斎之」<ref name="Asoshi" />}}</blockquote>

The other is the ''Ōhōri-ke Jinshi Keizu'' (大祝家神氏系図), a genealogy of the Suwa clan discovered in the ''Ōhōri''<nowiki />'s residence in 1884 ({{ill|Meiji era|en|Meiji era|qid=Q3125096|lt=Meiji}} 17).<ref>Kanai, Tenbi (2018). ''Suwa shinkō no seikaku to sono hensen: Suwa shinko tsūshi''. in Kodai Buzoku Kenkyūkai, ed. pp. 38-41.</ref><ref>Ihara (2008). p. 261.</ref><ref name="Miwakeizu">''Ōhōri-bon Jinshi Keizu'', cited in Kanai (1982). pp. 107, 190.</ref> It portrays Arikazu as a descendant of Kumako, the priest chosen by Takeminakata:

<blockquote>When Kumako was eight years old, the revered deity appeared, took off his robe and put them on Kumako. After declaring, "I do not have a body and so make you my body," he disappeared.{{efn|Literally: 'hid himself'}} This [Kumako] is the ancestor of Arikazu of the Miwa/Jin (Suwa) clan, the ''Misogihōri''. In the second year of Emperor Yōmei, Kumako built a sanctuary at the foot of the mountain at the southern side of the lake.
{{efn|「国造九世之孫、五百足、常時敬事于尊神、一日夢有神告、汝妻兄弟部既姙、身分娩必挙于男子、成長欲吾将有憑之、汝宜鍾愛矣夢覚而後、語之妻兄弟部、兄弟部亦同夢恠、且慎、後果而産男子因名神子、亦云熊子、神子八歳之時、尊神化現、脱着御衣於神子、吾無体以汝為体、有神勅隠御体矣、是則御衣着祝神氏有員之始祖也、用命天皇御宇二年、神子搆社壇于湖南山麓、其子神代、其子弟兄子、其子国積、其子猪麿、其子狭田野、其子高牧、亦云豊麿、其子生足、其子繁魚、其子豊足、亦云清主、其子有員、亦云武麿、」<ref name="Miwakeizu" />}}</blockquote>

====The King of Hadai====
A medieval Buddhist legend portrays Suwa Myōjin as a king from India who later achieved enlightenment and went to Japan [[Honji suijaku|to become a native ''kami'']].

A short text attached to a late 15th century copy of an ordinance regulating the Upper Shrine's ritual purity [[taboo]]s (物忌み ''monoimi'') originally enforced in 1238 and revised in 1317, the ''Suwa Kamisha monoimi no rei no koto'' (諏訪上社物忌令之事),<ref name="TakeiMasahiro">{{cite journal|last1=Takei|first1=Masahiro|title=祭事を読む-諏訪上社物忌令之事- (Saiji wo yomu: Suwa Kamisha monoimi no rei no koto)|journal=飯田市美術博物館 研究紀要 (Bulletin of the Iida City Museum)|date=1999|volume=9|pages=121–144|url=http://ci.nii.ac.jp/naid/110008434555}}</ref> relates that 'Takeminakata Myōjin' (武御名方明神) was originally the ruler of [[Mahajanapada|a certain Indian kingdom]] called 'Hadai' (波堤国 ''Hadai-koku''){{efn|This place name appears as one of the sixteen [[Mahajanapada|Mahājanapadas]] in {{ill|Kumārajīva|en|Kumārajīva|qid=Q335293|lt=Kumārajīva}}'s translation of the {{ill|Humane King Sutra|en|Humane King Sutra|qid=Q5939265|lt=Humane King Sutra}}.<ref>{{cite web|title=十六大国一覧表|url=http://www.sakya-muni.jp/pdf/mono15_s02_hu01.pdf|website=原始仏教聖典資料による釈尊伝の研究 (A Study of the Biography of Sakya-muni Based on the Early Buddhist Scriptural Sources)}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=佛說仁王般若波羅蜜經 第2卷|url=http://tripitaka.cbeta.org/T08n0245_002|website=CBETA (Chinese Buddhist Electronic Text Association) 漢文大藏經}}</ref>}} who survived an insurrection instigated by a rebel named 'Moriya' (守屋 or 守洩) during the king's absence while the latter was out hunting deer. After going to [[:en:Persia|Persia]] to rescue its inhabitants from an evil dragon, the king ruled over it for some time as 'Emperor Suwa' (陬波皇帝 ''Suwa Kōtei'') before retiring to "cultivate the seedling of virtue {{ill|Enlightenment in Buddhism|en|Enlightenment in Buddhism|qid=Q1137019|lt=and realize the Buddhist path}}." He eventually manifested in Japan, appearing in various places before finally choosing to dwell in Suwa.<ref name="chusei">Fukuda; Nihonmatsu; Tokuda, eds. (2015). pp. 114-116.</ref><ref name="Takei129130">Takei (1999), pp. 129–130.</ref><ref name="Miyachi84">Miyaji (1931b).  p. 84.</ref>

[[File:御射山神社鳥居 - panoramio.jpg|thumb|left|Misayama Shrine (御射山神社) in {{ill|Fujimi, Nagano|en|Fujimi, Nagano|qid=Q1204145|lt=Fujimi}}, Nagano. During the medieval period, the hunting ceremony held at Misayama - Suwa Shrine's sacred hunting ground - was the largest of Suwa's religious ceremonies and one of its most important, attracting thousands of people.]]

The ''Suwa Daimyōjin Ekotoba'' relates a slightly different, fuller version of the first half of this story as an origin myth for the Upper Shrine's hunting ceremony held every seventh month of the year at Misayama (御射山) on the slopes of the [[Yatsugatake Mountains]]:

<blockquote>If one should inquire about the origins (因縁 ''in'en'', lit. 'causes and conditions') of this hunt: long ago, the Daimyōjin was the king of the land of Hadai in {{ill|Tianzhu (India)|en|Tianzhu (India)|qid=Q3179625|lt=India}} who went out to hunt at {{ill|Sarnath|en|Sarnath|qid=Q324394|lt=Deer Park}} from the twenty-seventh to the thirtieth day of {{ill|Chinese calendar|en|Chinese calendar|qid=Q134032|lt=the seventh month}}. At that time, a traitorous vassal named Bikyō (美教) suddenly organized an army and sought to kill the king. The king, ringing a golden bell, looked up to heaven and shouted eight times: "I am now about to be killed by this rebel. I have hunted animals, not for my own enjoyment, but in order to lead them to the Buddhist path. If this my action is in accordance with Heaven's will, may [[:en:Brahmā|Brahmā]] save me."<br />
Brahmā then saw this and commanded the [[Four Heavenly Kings|four great deva-kings]] to wield {{ill|Vajra|en|Vajra|qid=Q695709|lt=Vajra}}-poles and destroy the army. It is said that the Misayama (三齋山) of today reflects that event.<br /> ... One should know, therefore, that the deity's compassionate hunting is an {{ill|Upaya|en|Upaya|qid=Q581473|lt=expedient means}} for the salvation of creatures.<ref>Translation based on Grumbach (2005). p. 210.</ref></blockquote>

Regarding the Upper Shrine's hunting rituals, the ''Monoimi no rei'' asserts that

<blockquote>[The shrine's] hunts began in the deer park of Hadai-no-kuni [in India]. [The use of] hawks began in [[Magadha|Magada-no-kuni]].<ref>Grumbach (2005). p. 206.</ref></blockquote>

[[File:Shaka Nyorai.jpg|thumb|120px|Medieval Buddhist legends claim the Suwa deity to be a relative of [[:en:Gautama Buddha|Gautama Buddha]] (pictured)]]
The second half of the legend (the slaying of the dragon in Persia and the king's migration to Japan) is used by the ''Ekotoba''<nowiki />'s compiler, Suwa Enchū, in a liturgical text, the ''Suwa Daimyōjin Kōshiki'' (諏方大明神講式),<ref name="Koshikitaikei">諏方大明神講式 (''Suwa Daimyōjin Kōshiki''), in {{cite book|editor1-last=Takeuchi|editor1-first=Hideo|title=神道大系 神社編30 諏訪 (Shintō Taikei, Jinja-hen vol. 30: Suwa)|date=1982|publisher=Shintō Taikei Hensankai}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=諏方大明神講式 (''Suwa Daimyōjin Kōshiki'')|url=http://base1.nijl.ac.jp/iview/Frame.jsp?DB_ID=G0003917KTM&C_CODE=KSRM-287105&IMG_SIZE=&PROC_TYPE=null&SHOMEI=%E3%80%90%E8%AB%8F%E6%96%B9%E5%A4%A7%E6%98%8E%EF%A8%99%E8%AC%9B%E5%BC%8F%E3%80%91&REQUEST_MARK=null&OWNER=null&IMG_NO=4|website=国文学研究資料館 (National Institute of Japanese Literature)}}</ref><ref name="chusei" /> where it is introduced as an alternative, if somewhat less credible, account of the Suwa deity's origins (in comparison to the myth of Takeminakata of Izumo as found in the ''Kuji Hongi'', touted by the same text as the authoritative origin story of the god) that nevertheless should not be suppressed.<ref>Fukuda; Nihonmatsu; Tokuda, eds. (2015). p. 116.</ref> In this text, the king of Hadai is claimed to be a great-great-grandson of {{ill|Sihahanu|en|Sihahanu|qid=Q7513387|lt=King Siṃhahanu}} (獅子頬王 ''Shishikyō-ō''), [[:en:Gautama Buddha|Gautama Buddha]]'s grandfather.<ref>Fukuda; Nihonmatsu; Tokuda, eds. (2015). p. 115.</ref> Bikyō, the rebel who raised up an army against the king in India - identified as an incarnation of the {{ill|Mara (demon)|en|Mara (demon)|qid=Q1352021|lt=Demon King}} (魔王) - is also said to have eventually manifested in Japan, opposing the deity in Suwa as "Moriya the evil outlaw."<ref>Fukuda; Nihonmatsu; Tokuda, eds. (2015). pp. 114-115.</ref>

A similar account appears in a work known as the ''Suwa Jinja Engi'' (諏訪神社縁起) or ''Suwa Shintō Engi'' (諏訪神道縁起),<ref>''Suwa Jinja Engi'' (諏訪神社縁起 上下卷), in {{cite book |editor1-last=Suwa Kyōikukai |title=諏訪史料叢書 巻26 (Suwa Shiryō Soshō, vol. 26) |date=1937 |publisher=Suwa Kōikukai |pages=54–64 |url=http://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/1185900/41}}</ref> wherein the Suwa deity is identified as the son of Kibonnō (貴飯王), the son of Amṛtodana (甘呂飯王 ''Kanrobonnō''), one of Siṃhahanu's four sons. The Lower Shrine's goddess, meanwhile, is the daughter of {{ill|Pasenadi|en|Pasenadi|qid=Q3055324|lt=Prasenajit}} (波斯匿王 ''Hashinoku-ō''), claimed here to be the son of Dronodana (黒飯王 ''Kokubonnō''), another son of Siṃhananu.<ref>Miyaji (1931b). p. 85.</ref>

=====The ''Suwa Mishirushibumi''=====

During the Misayama festival as performed during the medieval period, the ''Ōhōri'' recited a [[Norito|ritual declaration]] supposedly composed by the Suwa deity himself known as the ''Suwa Mishirushibumi'' (陬波御記文),<ref>Text and commentary in Kanai (1982). pp. 162-172.</ref> which begins:

<blockquote>I, Great King Suwa (陬波大王), have hidden my person during [[Sexagenary cycle|[the year/month/day of] the Yang Wood Horse]] (甲午 ''kinoe-uma'').<br />
[The name] 'Suwa' (陬波) and [the sign] Yang Wood Horse [and] the seal (印文){{efn|The 'seal' referred to here is interpreted to be either the Upper Shrine's sacred seal made of deer antler<ref>Kanai (1982). p. 167.</ref> or the ''Mishirushibumi'' itself.<ref>Fukuda; Nihonmatsu; Tokuda, eds. (2015). pp. 117-118.</ref>}} - these three are all one and the same.{{efn|「陬波大王　限甲午隠身、陬波与甲午　印文同一物三名。」<ref>Kanai (1982). p. 163.</ref>}}</blockquote>
[[File:Yabusame00.jpg|thumb|left|[[Yabusame]] archers in hunting gear, Edo period]]
Within the text, King Suwa (i.e. Suwa Myōjin) declares the ''Ōhōri'' to be his 'true [[Shintai|body]]' (真神体 ''shin no shintai'') and the Misayama (三斎山) hunting grounds below Yatsugatake (here likened to {{ill|Vulture Peak|en|Vulture Peak|qid=Q19755572|lt=Vulture Peak}} in India) to be another manifestation of himself that cleanses (斎) the three (三) evils: {{ill|Manasa, vacha, karmana|en|Manasa, vacha, karmana|qid=Q16920548|lt=evil thoughts, evil speech and evil actions}}.<ref>Fukuda; Nihonmatsu; Tokuda, eds. (2015). pp. 119-120.</ref><ref>Kanai (1982). pp. 168-169.</ref> He promises that whoever sets foot at Misayama will not fall into [[Saṃsāra (Buddhism)#Realms of rebirth|the lower, evil realms of existence]] (悪趣 ''akushu''); conversely, the god condemns and disowns whoever defiles the hunting grounds by cutting down its trees or digging out the soil.<ref name="Kanai169">Kanai (1982). p. 169.</ref>

A commentary on the ''Mishirushibumi'', the ''Suwa Shichū'' (陬波私注 "Personal Notes on the ''Suwa Mishirusibumi''," written 1313–1314),<ref name="KanaiShichu">Text and commentary in Kanai (1982). pp. 173-187.</ref> elaborates on the text by retelling the legend of Suwa Myōjin's consecration of his first priest:

<blockquote>The ''Daimyōjin'' was born during [the year/month/day of] the Yang Wood Horse and disappeared during [the year/month/day of] the Yang Wood Horse.<br />
Sokutan Daijin (続旦大臣) was the Daimyōjin's uncle who accompanied him from India. When the Daimyōjin was to disappear, he took off his garments, put them on the Daijin, and dubbed him the ''Misogihōri'' (御衣木法理). He then pronounced a vow: "You shall consider this priest to be my body."{{efn|「一、大明神甲午<sub>仁</sub>有御誕生甲午<sub>仁</sub>隠御身給<sub>フ</sub><br />
一、続旦（ソクタン）大臣<small>ト</small>申<small>ハ</small>大明神<small>ノ</small>叔父御前自<sub>リ</sub>天竺御同道、大明神御体<sub>ヲ</sub>隠<sub>サセ</sub>給<sub>シ</sub>時御装束ヲ奉抜著（ヌキキセ）彼大臣給<small>テ</small>号御衣木（ミソキ）法理<small>ト</small> 我之躰以法理<small>ヲ</small>躰<small>ト</small>セヨトハ誓給<sub>シ</sub>也」<ref>Kanai (1982). pp. 173-174.</ref>}}</blockquote>

The same text identifies the god's uncle Sokutan Daijin with Arikazu.<ref>Fukuda; Nihonmatsu; Tokuda, eds. (2015). pp. 117, 119.</ref><ref>Kanai (1982). pp. 176-177.</ref>{{efn|「一、御衣木法理殿御実名<sub>ハ</sub>者有員<sub>云〻</sub>」<ref>Kanai (1982). p. 175.</ref>}}

====Suwa Myōjin and the frog god====
[[File:Kawazugari (Frog Hunting) Ritual - 蛙狩神事.jpg|thumb|The Frog Hunting Ritual of Suwa Shrine (taken before 1937)]]
Two texts, the ''Monoimi no rei''<ref>Kanai (1982). pp. 165.</ref><ref>Takei (1999), p. 134.</ref> and the ''Suwa Shichū'' (陬波私注 "Personal Notes on the ''Suwa Mishirusibumi''," written 1313–1314),<ref name="KanaiShichu"/> mention an oral legend about Suwa Myōjin pacifying the waves of the {{ill|Four Seas|en|Four Seas|qid=Q10925152|lt=four seas}} by subduing an unruly {{ill|Frog|en|Frog|qid=Q53636|lt=Frog}} god.

<blockquote>Suwa (陬波) should be read as "the waves are calm." When a frog god (蝦蟆神), being a harmful god (荒神 ''{{ill|Kōjin|en|Kōjin|qid=Q6455190|lt=Kōjin}}''), caused suffering to [[Tianxia#Japan|the realm]], the ''Daimyōjin'' quelled it and came to reside here; [because] the {{ill|Four Seas|en|Four Seas|qid=Q10925152|lt=four seas}} were calm, it is called Suwa.{{efn|「一、陬波<sub>ト</sub>申事<sub>ナミシツカナリトヨメリ</sub>　蝦蟆<sub>カニタ</sub>神<sup>カエルノ事ナリ</sup>荒神惱<sub>ト</sub>天下時、大明神退治之御坐時 四海静謐之間 陬波<sub>卜云〻</sub> 口傅在之」}}<ref>Translation from Grumbach (2005). p. 172.</ref></blockquote>

After defeating this frog, Suwa Myōjin then blocked the way to its dwelling - a hole leading to the underwater palace of the [[Ryūjin|dragon god of the sea]], the [[Ryūgū-jō]] - with a rock and sat on it.<ref name="KanaiShichu" /><ref>Kanai (1982). pp. 165, 177-179.</ref><ref name="Takei136137">Takei (1999), p. 136-137.</ref>

This story functions as an {{ill|Etiology|en|Etiology|qid=Q156318|lt=etiological legend}} for the annual sacrifice of frogs held every [[Japanese New Year|New Year's Day]] in the Upper Shrine ([[#As god of hunting|see below]])<ref>Miyasaka (1992). p. 20</ref> as well as yet another {{ill|Folk etymology|en|Folk etymology|qid=Q109964|lt=Folk etymology}} for the toponym 'Suwa' (rendered here as 陬波), here explained as deriving either from a term for a wave lapping onto the sea's edge<ref name="Kanai177178">Kanai (1982). pp. 177-178.</ref> or a reference to the deity's pacification of the waters: "the waves are calm."<ref>Grumbach (2005). p. 172.</ref>

The portrayal of Suwa Myōjin's enemy as a frog also hints at the deity's character as a serpentine water god.<ref name="Kanai177178" /> (As a point of comparison, the obscure snake god [[Ugajin]] was also credited with defeating a malevolent frog deity.<ref name="Hara2012">{{cite book|last1=Hara|first1=Naomasa|title=龍蛇神: 諏訪大明神の中世的展開 (Ryūjashin: Suwa Daimyōjin no chūseiteki tenkai)|date=2012|publisher=Ningensha|isbn=978-4931388710|pages=40–41|language=ja}}</ref>) The frog god itself has been interpreted either as representing the native deities [[Mishaguji]] and/or Moriya, with its defeat symbolizing the victory of the cult of Suwa Myōjin over the indigenous belief system,<ref>Takei (1999). pp. 137-138.</ref><ref>Kanai (1982). p. 68.</ref> or as a symbol of the Buddhist concept of the {{ill|Three poisons|en|Three poisons|qid=Q683151|lt=Three poisons}} (ignorance, greed, and hatred), which Suwa Myōjin, as [[Honji suijaku|an incarnation]] of the bodhisattva {{ill|Samantabhadra (Bodhisattva)|en|Samantabhadra (Bodhisattva)|qid=Q868306|lt=Samantabhadra}}, his esoteric aspect {{ill|Vajrasattva|en|Vajrasattva|qid=Q2380086|lt=Vajrasattva}} and the [[Wisdom King]] {{ill|Trailokyavijaya|en|Trailokyavijaya|qid=Q532825|lt=Trailokyavijaya}} (interpreted as a manifestation of Vajrasattva), is said to destroy.<ref name="Hara2012" />

====The dragon (serpent) deity of Suwa====
[[File:Suwa taisha Kamisha Honmiya , 諏訪大社 上社 本宮 - panoramio (30).jpg|thumb|left|''{{ill|Chōzuya|en|Chōzuya|qid=Q1069667|lt=Chōzuya}}'' with a dragon-shaped spout, ''Kamisha Honmiya'']]
Folk belief has long held the god of Suwa Shrine to assume the form of a serpent or dragon. Consequently, the deity appears as such in a number of folktales and anecdotes.

In one such story, Suwa Myōjin once came to {{ill|Izumo Province|en|Izumo Province|qid=Q582846|lt=Izumo Province}} in the form of a dragon so gigantic that only his head can be seen; his tail was still at Suwa, caught in a tall pine tree by the shores of the lake. The other gods, upon seeing him, were so astounded and frightened at his enormous size that they exempted him from attending their yearly meetings.<ref>Matsutani, Miyoko (1960). ''Shinano no minwa'' (信濃の民話). Miraisha. p. 48, cited in Kanai (1982). p. 7.</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Shinano no kuni no Kannazuki (信濃の国の神無月)|url=http://minwa.fujipan.co.jp/area/nagano_012/|website=Fuji Baking Co., Ltd.|access-date=January 5, 2017|archive-date=January 5, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170105180141/http://minwa.fujipan.co.jp/area/nagano_012/|url-status=dead}}</ref> Thus, the deity of Suwa is claimed to be one of the very few ''kami'' in Japan who do not leave their shrines during the month of [[Kannazuki]], when most gods are thought to gather at Izumo and thus are absent from most of the country. The supposed tree where the dragon's tail was caught (currently reduced to a stump) is locally known as {{nihongo|''Okakematsu''|尾掛松}}.<ref>{{cite web|title=Okakematsu (尾掛松)|url=http://suwaarea-examine.com/okakematu.html|website=Mahoroba Suwa-ken (まほろば諏訪圏)|access-date=2015-01-05}}</ref>

A variant of this story transposes the setting from Izumo to the [[Kyoto Imperial Palace|Imperial Palace]] in {{ill|Kyoto|en|Kyoto|qid=Q34600|lt=Kyoto}}; in this version, the various ''kami'' are said to travel to the ancient capital every [[Japanese New Year|New Year's Day]] to greet the emperor.<ref>Ōbayashi, Taryō (1987). "Seikūkan no kōsei genri. Bunka-jinruigaku no shiten kara (聖空間の構成原理―文化人類学の視点から)." In {{cite book|author1=Ueda|author2=Gorai|author3=Ōbayashi|author4=Miyasaka, M.|author5=Miyasaka, Y.|title=Onbashira-sai to Suwa-taisha|pages=97–98}}</ref>

Another popular story promulgated by wandering preachers associated with the shrines of Suwa during the medieval period claimed the Suwa deity to have originally been [[Kōga Saburō]], a warrior who temporarily became a dragon or a snake after a journey into the underworld.<ref>Miyasaka (1987). pp. 51-54.</ref><ref name="BreenTeeuwen2000">{{cite book|author1=John Breen|author2=Mark Teeuwen|title=Shinto in History: Ways of the Kami|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=MADlfH002mAC&pg=PA35|date=January 2000|publisher=University of Hawaii Press|isbn=978-0-8248-2363-4|page=35}}</ref><ref name="Blacker2004">{{cite book|author=Carmen Blacker|title=The Catalpa Bow: A Study of Shamanistic Practices in Japan|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=mR6PAgAAQBAJ&pg=RA1-PA134|date=2 August 2004|publisher=Routledge|isbn=1-135-31872-7}}</ref><ref>Kanai (1982). pp. 278–317.</ref>

====''Omiwatari''====
[[File:180205 Lake Suwa omiwatari 03.jpg|thumb|''Omiwatari'']]
{{ill|Pressure ridge (ice)|en|Pressure ridge (ice)|qid=Q3134007|lt=Cracks and ridges}} that form on a frozen {{ill|Lake Suwa|en|Lake Suwa|qid=Q1206692|lt=Lake Suwa}} during cold winters have traditionally been interpreted as the trail left behind by Suwa Myōjin as he leaves the ''Upper Shrine'' and crosses the lake to meet his wife enshrined on the Lower Shrine on the opposite (northern) shore.<ref name="railways1922">{{cite book|author=Japan. Dept. of railways|title=The Hot Springs of Japan (and the Principal Cold Springs) Including Chosen (Korea) Taiwan (Formosa) South Manchuria, Together with Many Tables Giving Classification, Chemical Basis, Curative Values, Radio-activity, Etc. 196 Illustrations, 15 Maps, Specially Drawn, 2 Colored Lithographs|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=smA0AAAAMAAJ|year=1922|page=194}}</ref> Called ''Omiwatari'' (御神渡 'the god's crossing' or 'the god's pathway'), the cracks were considered to be a good omen for the coming year.<ref name="JapanTimes">{{cite news|title=Ice phenomenon warms up hearts in the Lake Suwa region|url=http://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2012/03/03/national/ice-phenomenon-warms-up-hearts-in-the-lake-suwa-region/#.WRpvc9SLRRA|agency=The Japan Times|date=2012-03-03}}</ref> The priests of the Grand Shrine of Suwa traditionally used the crack's appearance to divine the quality of the year's harvest.<ref name="Miyasaka3840">Miyasaka (1992). pp. 38-40.</ref> For the locals, the crack also served as a sign that the frozen lake was safe to walk upon.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Brazil|first1=Mark|title=Omi-watari|url=http://www.japanvisitor.com/about-japan/omi-watari|website=Japan Visitor}}</ref><ref>Miyasaka (1992). p. 42.</ref> Conversely, the ''omiwatari''<nowiki/>'s failure to appear at all (明海 ''ake no umi'') or the cracks forming in an unusual way were held to be a sign of bad luck for the year.<ref name="Miyasaka3840" />

Since the late 20th century, the ''omiwatari'' has become a much rarer sight than it was in the past due to rising temperatures caused by {{ill|Global warming|en|Global warming|qid=Q7942|lt=Global warming}}.<ref name="JapanTimes" /><ref>{{cite book|editor1-last=Ichikawa|editor1-first=Atsunobu|title=Global Warming — The Research Challenges: A Report of Japan's Global Warming Initiative|date=2013|publisher=Springer Science & Business Media|isbn=978-1402029417|pages=34–35|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=uXNHBAAAQBAJ&pg=PT34}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|last1=Borre|first1=Lisa|title=Lake Suwa's Shinto Legend and the Oldest Lake Ice Record on Earth: What It Tells Us About Climate Change and Variability|url=http://voices.nationalgeographic.com/2016/04/26/lake-suwas-shinto-legend-and-the-oldest-lake-ice-record-on-earth-what-it-tells-us-about-climate-change-and-variability/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160426213200/http://voices.nationalgeographic.com/2016/04/26/lake-suwas-shinto-legend-and-the-oldest-lake-ice-record-on-earth-what-it-tells-us-about-climate-change-and-variability/|url-status=dead|archive-date=April 26, 2016|website=National Geographic|date=August 30, 2023 }}</ref>

====As god of war====
[[File:Sakanoue Tamuramaro sw.jpg|thumb|150px|left|[[Sakanoue no Tamuramaro]] is credited with instituting the religious festivities of Suwa Shrine after the god of Suwa came to his aid against the {{ill|Emishi|en|Emishi|qid=Q932574|lt=Emishi}} peoples.]]
Suwa Myōjin is also considered to be a {{ill|List of war deities|en|List of war deities|qid=Q1752560|lt=god of war}}, one of a number of such deities in the Japanese pantheon. The ''[[:en:Songs to Make the Dust Dance on the Beams|Ryōjin Hishō]]'' compiled in 1179 (the late {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|qid=Q193292|lt=Heian period}}) also attest to the worship of the god of Suwa in the capacity of god of warfare at the time of its compilation, naming the shrine of Suwa among famous shrines to martial deities in the eastern half of the country.{{Blockquote|text=<poem>These gods of war live [[:en:Kantō|east of the barrier]]:{{efn|During the Heian period, the expression 'east of the barrier' (関の東 ''seki-no-hi(n)gashi'', whence derives the term 関東 ''Kantō'') referred to the provinces beyond the checkpoints or barrier stations (関 ''seki'') at the eastern fringes of {{ill|Kinai|en|Kinai|qid=Q906708|lt=the capital region}}, more specifically the land east of the checkpoint at Ōsaka/Ausaka Hill (逢坂 'hill of meeting', old orthography: ''Afusaka''; not to be confused with the modern city of {{ill|Osaka|en|Osaka|qid=Q35765|lt=Osaka}}) in modern {{ill|Ōtsu|en|Ōtsu|qid=Q202907|lt=Ōtsu}}, {{ill|Shiga Prefecture|en|Shiga Prefecture|qid=Q131358|lt=Shiga Prefecture}}.<ref name="books.google.com">{{cite book|last1=Marshall|first1=Yuko|title=Heterogeneous Japan: The Cultural Distinctions Between Western and Eastern Japan|date=2008|page=6|isbn=9780549562146|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=8EdvhO4Xkn4C&pg=PA6|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170215161620/https://books.google.com/books?id=8EdvhO4Xkn4C&pg=PA6|url-status=dead|archive-date=February 15, 2017}}</ref> By the Edo period, ''Kantō'' was reinterpreted to mean the region east of the checkpoint in {{ill|Hakone|en|Hakone|qid=Q671040|lt=Hakone}}, {{ill|Kanagawa Prefecture|en|Kanagawa Prefecture|qid=Q127513|lt=Kanagawa Prefecture}}.}}
[[Kashima Jingū|Kashima]], [[Katori Jingū|Katori]], Suwa no Miya, and [[Shirahige Shrine|Hira Myōjin]];
also [[Awa Shrine|Su]] in {{ill|Awa Province (Chiba)|en|Awa Province (Chiba)|qid=Q1053044|lt=Awa}}, [[:ja:下立松原神社|Otaka Myōjin]] in {{ill|Shirahama, Chiba|en|Shirahama, Chiba|qid=Q1951937|lt=Tai no Kuchi}},
[[Kusanagi no Tsurugi|Yatsurugi]] in [[:en:Atsuta Jingu|Atsuta]], and [[Tado Taisha|Tado no Miya]] in {{ill|Ise Province|en|Ise Province|qid=Q864166|lt=Ise}}.</poem>|title=''Ryōjin Hishō''|source=song 258<ref name="University of California Press">{{cite book|last1=Kim|first1=Yung-Hee|title=Songs to Make the Dust Dance: The Ryōjin Hishō of Twelfth-century Japan|date=1994|publisher=University of California Press|location=Berkeley|isbn=978-0-520-08066-9|pages=144–145a|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=SFlSLX-nCeEC&pg=PA144}}</ref> {{efn|「関より東(ひむかし)の軍神(いくさがみ)、鹿島・香取(かんどり)・諏訪の宮、また比良(ひら)の明神、安房の洲(す)滝(たい)の口や小鷹明神、熱田に八剣(やつるぎ)、伊勢には多度(たど)の宮。」}}}}

During the medieval period, legends claiming Suwa Myōjin to have appeared and provided assistance to eminent figures such as {{ill|Empress Jingū|en|Empress Jingū|qid=Q232803|lt=Empress Jingū}}<ref>Ota (1926). pp. 160-164.</ref> or the general [[Sakanoue no Tamuramaro]]<ref>諏訪大明神秋山祭の事 (''Suwa Daimyōjin Akiyama-sai no koto''), in Kishi (1967). pp. 49–56.</ref><ref name="Konishi">{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=szAABAAAQBAJ&pg=PA526|title=A History of Japanese Literature, Volume 3: The High Middle Ages|last1=Konishi|first1=Jin'ichi|date=2014|publisher=Princeton University Press|isbn=978-1400861828|page=526}}</ref><ref>Fukuda; Nihonmatsu; Tokuda, eds. (2015). pp. 124-127.</ref> during their respective military campaigns circulated.

The god of Suwa was also credited with the attempted {{ill|Mongol invasions of Japan|en|Mongol invasions of Japan|qid=Q208156|lt=Mongol invasions of Japan}} under {{ill|Kublai Khan|en|Kublai Khan|qid=Q7523|lt=Kublai Khan}}. The ''[[Taiheiki]]'' recounts a story where a five-colored cloud resembling a serpent (a manifestation of the god) rose up from {{ill|Lake Suwa|en|Lake Suwa|qid=Q1206692|lt=Lake Suwa}} and spread away westward to assist the Japanese army against the Mongols.<ref>De Visser (1913). p. 202.</ref><ref>Ōbayashi (1987). p. 96.</ref>

<blockquote>On the seventh day, when the Imperial devotions were completed, from Lake Suwa there arose a cloud of many colours, in shape like a great serpent, which spread away towards the west. The doors of the Temple-treasury of [[Hachiman]] flew open, and the skies were filled with a sound of galloping horses and of ringing bits.
