In {{ill|Hiyoshi Taisha|en|Hiyoshi Taisha|qid=Q656451|lt=the twenty-one shrines of Yoshino}} the brocade-curtained mirrors moved, the swords of the Temple-treasury put on a sharp edge, and all the shoes offered to the god turned towards the west. At [[:en:Sumiyoshi taisha|Sumiyoshi]] sweat poured from below the saddles of the four horses sacred to the deities, and the iron shields turned of themselves and faced the enemy in a line.<ref>{{cite web|title=太平記 巻第三十九|url=http://j-texts.com/taihei/tk39.html|website=J-TEXTS 日本文学電子図書館|date=December 30, 2020 }}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last1=Aston|first1=William George|title=A History of Japanese Literature|date=2015|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-1108081061|page=181|edition=reprint|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xxxoBgAAQBAJ&pg=PA181}}</ref></blockquote>

==Analysis==
===Takeminakata in the ''Kojiki''===
[[Image:Ono-Yasumaro.jpg|thumb|right|{{ill|Ō no Yasumaro|en|Ō no Yasumaro|qid=Q384705|lt=Ō no Yasumaro}}, the compiler of the ''Kojiki'']]

Takeminakata's abrupt appearance in the ''Kojiki''<nowiki />'s version of the ''kuni-yuzuri'' myth has long puzzled scholars, as the god is mentioned nowhere else in the work, including the genealogy of Ōkuninushi's progeny that precedes the ''kuni-yuzuri'' narrative proper.<ref>Chamberlain (1882). [http://sacred-texts.com/shi/kj/kj033.htm Section XXVI.—The Deities the August Descendants of the Deity Master-of-the-Great-Land.]</ref> Aside from the parallel account contained in the ''Kuji Hongi'' (which was itself based on the ''Kojiki''<ref name="Suwashishi2">Suwa Shishi Hensan Iinkai, ed. (1995). pp. 684-685, 687.</ref>), he is altogether absent from the ''Nihon Shoki''<nowiki />'s version of the myth.<ref>{{cite wikisource |Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697 |chapter=Book II |author=Aston, William George |date=1896 |pages=68–70}}</ref><ref>Miyasaka (1987). p. 18.</ref> Early documents from Izumo such as the province's ''[[Fudoki]]'' also fail to mention any god named '(Take)minakata', nor is there apparently any sign of Takeminakata worship in Izumo in antiquity.<ref name="Suwashishi2" />

Pre-modern authors such as {{ill|Motoori Norinaga|en|Motoori Norinaga|qid=Q384647|lt=Motoori Norinaga}} tended to explain Takeminakata's absence outside of the ''Kojiki'' and the ''Kuji Hongi'' by conflating the god with certain obscure deities found in other sources thought to share certain similar characteristics (e.g. [[Isetsuhiko]]).<ref name="Norinaga3">Motoori, Norinaga (1937). [http://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/1109355/81 古事記傳 (''Kojiki-den''), vol. 14] in Motoori Toyokai (ed.), 本居宣長全集 (''Motoori Norinaga Zenshū''), vol. 2. Tokyo: Yoshikawa Kōbunkan. pp. 683–684. (Original work written 1764–1798)</ref> While a few modern scholars still suppose some kind of indirect connection between the deity and Izumo by postulating that Takeminakata's origins lie either in peoples that migrated from Izumo northwards to Suwa and the {{ill|Hokuriku region|en|Hokuriku region|qid=Q381025|lt=Hokuriku region}}<ref>Muraoka (1969). pp. 60-66.</ref> or in Hokuriku itself (the ancient {{ill|Koshi Province (Japan)|en|Koshi Province (Japan)|qid=Q1351611|lt=province of Koshi}}, a region apparently once under Izumo's {{ill|Sphere of influence|en|Sphere of influence|qid=Q593682|lt=Sphere of influence}} as can be inferred from the myth of Ōkuninushi's marriage to Nunakawahime),<ref>Kanai (1982). pp. 8-9.</ref> others instead propose that the connection between Takeminakata and Izumo is an artificial construct by the ''Kojiki''<nowiki/>'s compilers.<ref name="Suwashishi2" /><ref name="Yoshii" /><ref name="Matsumae">{{cite book|author=Matsumae, Takeshi|title=Nihon shinwa no nazo ga yoku wakaru hon (日本神話の謎がよく分かる本)|date=2007|publisher=Daiwa Shobō (大和書房)|isbn=978-4-479-39166-1|pages=136–137}}</ref><ref name="miyachi90101">Miyaji (1931). pp. 90-101.</ref>

The contest between Takeminakata and Takemikazuchi - an element absent in other versions of the ''kuni-yuzuri'' myth cycle - is often explained as being either a new myth invented to serve the interests of the imperial court and the [[Fujiwara clan]], descendants of the [[Nakatomi clan]] that had worshiped Takemikazuchi as a [[Ujigami|patron deity]]<ref name="miyachi90101"/> (indeed, in other versions it is the god [[Futsunushi]] that takes center stage rather than Takemikazuchi, who is believed to have taken on Futsunushi's roles and attributes after the Nakatomi rose to power<ref>{{cite web |last1=Kadoya |first1=Atsushi |title=Futsunushi |url=http://eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp/modules/xwords/entry.php?entryID=54 |website=Encyclopedia of Shinto |publisher=Kokugakuin University |access-date=2019-07-08}}</ref>), or an adaptation/reversal of a myth concerning a battle between an interloping god and a local deity preserved in the Suwa region (see below), with Takeminakata (the invading conqueror in Suwa myth) being recast into the role of the subjugated earthly ''kami''.<ref>Miyasaka (1987). pp. 30-33.</ref>

=== Suwa Myōjin and Moriya ===
[[File:Yasaka-no-Suzu - 八栄の鈴.jpg|thumb|The ''yasaka no suzu'' (八栄の鈴), a set of bronze [[Suzu (bell)|bells]] reputed in legend to have been brought to Suwa by Suwa Myōjin. In actuality, the bells date from the early {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|qid=Q193292|lt=Heian period}}.]]
The myth of Takeminakata's (Suwa Myōjin's) arrival in Suwa and his defeat of the god Moriya has been interpreted as the mythicization of a historical event in which a local lineage of chieftains who ruled the Suwa area was subjugated by invading outsiders, who subsequently set themselves up as the new rulers of the region - all the while still retaining the subjugated clan in an important position as the wielder of spiritual and ritual authority. This theory explains the relation between the Suwa (Miwa/Jin) and Moriya priestly families of the Upper Shrine of Suwa as that of the Moriya clan being the regional power supplanted by the newly arrived Miwa (Suwa) clan.

[[File:Ina Valley Relief Map, SRTM.jpg|thumb|left|190px|Relief map of the Ina Valley. {{ill|Lake Suwa|en|Lake Suwa|qid=Q1206692|lt=Lake Suwa}} can be seen at top right.]]
While one theory places this event during the end of the [[Jōmon period]], thus portraying the new arrivals as {{ill|Agrarian society|en|Agrarian society|qid=Q396108|lt=agrarian}} {{ill|Yayoi people|en|Yayoi people|qid=Q19921451|lt=Yayoi}} tribes who came into conflict with indigenous {{ill|Jōmon people|en|Jōmon people|qid=Q11608110|lt=Jōmon}} hunter-gatherers,<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Tanaka|first1=Atsuko|script-title=ja:古社叢の「聖地」の構造（3）─諏訪大社の場合|journal=Journal of Kyoto Seika University|pages=122–123|url=http://www.kyoto-seika.ac.jp/researchlab/wp/wp-content/uploads/kiyo/pdf-data/no39/tanaka_atsuko.pdf|language=ja|access-date=November 9, 2019|archive-date=July 22, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210722115610/https://www.kyoto-seika.ac.jp/researchlab/wp/wp-content/uploads/kiyo/pdf-data/no39/tanaka_atsuko.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name="NHK">{{cite AV media|title=古代史ミステリー 「御柱」～最後の"縄文王国"の謎～ (Kodaishi Mystery. Onbashira: Saigo no Jōmon-ōkoku no nazo)|medium=Documentary|publisher=NHK|location=Japan|date=2016|url=http://www.nhk.or.jp/docudocu/program/46/2586790/|language=ja|access-date=November 9, 2019|archive-date=July 8, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190708025134/http://www.nhk.or.jp/docudocu/program/46/2586790/|url-status=dead}}</ref> others instead propose this conflict to have taken place during the late [[Kofun period]] (late 6th-early 7th century), when keyhole-shaped [[Kofun|Kofuns]] containing {{ill|Horse tack|en|Horse tack|qid=Q950799|lt=equestrian gear}} as grave goods - up to this point found mainly in the {{ill|Shimoina District, Nagano|en|Shimoina District, Nagano|qid=Q726999|lt=Shimoina region}} southwest of Suwa - begin to appear in the Lake Suwa area, replacing the kind of burial that had been common in the region since the early 5th century. This theory thus supposes these migrants to have been a clan allied with the {{ill|Yamato period|en|Yamato period|qid=Q633881|lt=Yamato kingdom}} that specialized in horse breeding and horseback riding. Indeed, the Yamato polity showed strong interest to Shinano because of its suitability as a place for grazing and breeding horses and considered it a strategic base for conquering the eastern regions.<ref>Miyasaka (1987). pp. 18-22.</ref><ref>Suwa Shishi Hensan Iinkai, ed. (1995). p. 692.</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Terada |first1=Shizuko |last2=Washio |first2=Tetsuta |title=諏訪明神―カミ信仰の原像 (Suwa Myōjin: Kami shinkō no genzō)|date=2010 |publisher=Iwata Shoin |pages=64–67, 134–136}}</ref><ref>Oh (2011). pp. 156-157, 161-162, 176.</ref> This clan, the Miwa (Suwa), is thought to be related to either the Kanasashi clan (金刺氏), an offshoot of a local magnate clan (''[[kuni no miyatsuko]]'') that later became the high priestly family of the Lower Shrine of Suwa,<ref>Suwa Shishi Hensan Iinkai, ed. (1995). pp. 615-623, 686-696.</ref> or the Miwa (Ōmiwa) clan ([[:ja:三輪氏|三輪氏]]) originally based on the area around {{ill|Mount Miwa|en|Mount Miwa|qid=Q860627|lt=Mount Miwa}} in {{ill|Yamato Province|en|Yamato Province|qid=Q907495|lt=Yamato Province}}.<ref>Terada; Washio (2010). pp. 136-138.</ref> The theory suggests based on archaeological evidence that the Miwa (Suwa) came to the Suwa Basin from Shimoina, making their way northwards along the [[Tenryū River]].<ref>Terada; Washio (2010). pp. 66-67, 134-136.</ref> In conjunction with this hypothesis, it is pointed out that in the ''Nobushige Gejō'' (believed to be the earliest attestation of this myth), the Suwa deity is said to have descended from heaven bringing with him bells, a {{ill|Bronze mirror|en|Bronze mirror|qid=Q1041984|lt=mirror}}, a {{ill|Saddle|en|Saddle|qid=Q192249|lt=Saddle}} and a {{ill|Bridle|en|Bridle|qid=Q148558|lt=Bridle}}.<ref>Grumbach (2005). p. 188.</ref><ref>Suwa Shishi Hensan Iinkai, ed. (1995). p. 683.</ref><ref>Miyasaka (1987). p. 33.</ref>

[[File:Mononobe no Moriya.jpg|thumb|150px|{{ill|Mononobe no Moriya|en|Mononobe no Moriya|qid=Q2424736|lt=Mononobe no Moriya}}]]
This theory that the legend of the Suwa deity's victory over Moriya reflects historical fact has recently come into question. Due to similarities between certain variants of this myth and medieval legends surrounding {{ill|Prince Shōtoku|en|Prince Shōtoku|qid=Q263972|lt=Prince Shōtoku}}'s defeat of {{ill|Mononobe no Moriya|en|Mononobe no Moriya|qid=Q2424736|lt=Mononobe no Moriya}} (e.g. Shōtoku's and Suwa Myōjin's opponents both being named 'Moriya', the deity's manifestation and the foundation of the Upper Shrine being dated to the year 587 - the same year as the {{ill|Soga–Mononobe conflict|en|Soga–Mononobe conflict|qid=Q534720|lt=battle}} between the [[Soga clan|Soga]] and the [[:en:Mononobe|Mononobe]] clans - in some texts), some see the myth as being highly influenced by such stories about Shōtoku (so Ihara, 2008),<ref>Ihara (2008). p. 161-162.</ref> while others regard it as an outright invention modeled on these legends (Harada, 2018).<ref>Harada (2018) p. 81.</ref> Aoki (2012) theorizes that the myth developed somewhere during the late Heian and early {{ill|Kamakura period|en|Kamakura period|qid=Q236205|lt=Kamakura}} periods, when the deity of Suwa came to be venerated as a warrior god, and cautions against uncritical application of this story to known archaeological data.<ref>Aoki (2012). pp. 26-31.</ref>

===Takeminakata in imperial sources===
While the ''Kojiki'' does not yet explicitly mention the worship of Takeminakata in Suwa, by the following century, we see the name applied to the god worshipped in what is now the Grand Shrine of Suwa: aside from the ''Kuji Hongi''<nowiki />'s (807-936 CE) reference to Takeminakata being enshrined in 'Suwa Shrine in Suwa {{ill|Districts of Japan|en|Districts of Japan|qid=Q1122846|lt=District}}'<ref name="Hongi" /><ref name="Hongi2" /> the ''[[Shoku Nihon Kōki]]'' mentions the deity 'Minakatatomi-no-Kami of Suwa District, Shinano Province' (信濃国諏訪郡 ... 南方刀美神) being promoted from Rankless (无位) to junior fifth Rank, lower grade (従五位下) by the imperial court in the year 842 CE ({{ill|Jōwa (Heian period)|en|Jōwa (Heian period)|qid=Q1075605|lt=Jōwa}} 9).{{efn|「丁未。奉授信濃國諏方郡无位勳八等南方刀美神從五位下。」}}<ref name="Shoku1">{{cite web|title=續日本後紀|url=http://www.j-texts.com/chuko/shokukouki.html|website=J－TEXTS 日本文学電子図書館}}</ref><ref name="Shoku2">{{cite wikisource |chapter=卷第十一 |wslink=zh:續日本後紀 |plaintitle=''[[Shoku Nihon Kōki]]'' (續日本後紀)}}</ref><ref name="Database">{{cite web|title=南方刀美神社二座（建御名方富命神）|url=http://21coe.kokugakuin.ac.jp/db/jinja/kindex2.php?J_ID=240101|website=神社資料データベース (Shinto Jinja Database)|publisher=Kokugakuin University}}</ref><ref name="Suwa689">Suwa Shishi Hensan Iinkai, ed. (1995). p. 689.</ref>

During the 850-60s, Takeminakata and his shrine rose very rapidly in Rank (''[[Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku|Montoku Jitsuroku]]'', ''[[Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku]]''), being promoted to the Rank of junior fifth, upper grade (従五位上) in 850 ({{ill|Kashō|en|Kashō|qid=Q1373157|lt=Kashō}} 3),{{efn|「己未。信濃國御名方富命神、健御名方富命前八坂刀賣命神、並加從五位上。」}}<ref name="Montoku">{{cite wikisource |chapter=卷第二 |wslink=zh:日本文德天皇實錄 |plaintitle=''[[Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku]]'' (日本文德天皇實錄)}}</ref> to junior third (従三位) in 851 ({{ill|Ninju|en|Ninju|qid=Q1373077|lt=Ninju}} 1),{{efn|「乙丑。進信濃國建御名方富命、前八坂刀賣命等兩大神階、加從三位。」}}<ref name="Montoku2">{{cite wikisource |chapter=卷第三 |wslink=zh:日本文德天皇實錄 |plaintitle=''[[Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku]]'' (日本文德天皇實錄)}}</ref> to junior (従二位){{efn|「廿七日甲申。 (...) 信濃國正三位勳八等建御名方冨命神從二位。」}} and then senior second (正二位){{efn|「十一日丁酉。(...) 授信濃國從二位勳八等建御名方富命神正二位。」}} in 859 ({{ill|Jōgan|en|Jōgan|qid=Q1075635|lt=Jōgan}} 1),<ref name="NihonSandai">{{cite wikisource |chapter=卷第十 |wslink=zh:日本三代實錄 |plaintitle=''[[Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku]]'' (日本三代實錄)}}</ref> and finally to junior first Rank (従一位) in 867 (Jōgan 9).{{efn|「十一日辛亥。信濃國正二位勳八等建御名方富命神進階從一位。」}}<ref name="NihonSandai2">{{cite wikisource |chapter=卷第十四 |wslink=zh:日本三代實錄 |plaintitle=''[[Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku]]'' (日本三代實錄)}}</ref><ref name="Database" /> The influence of the Kanasashi-no-toneri clan is thought to be behind the deity's sudden progress in Rank.<ref name="Suwa689" /><ref name="Owa221">Ōwa (1990). p. 221-223.</ref>

After a few decades, the 'Register of Deities' (神名帳 ''Jinmyōchō'') section of the ''[[Engishiki]]'' (927) speaks of the 'Minakatatomi Shrine(s)' (南方刀美神社) as enshrining two deities and being the two {{ill|Myōjin|en|Myōjin|qid=Q5369590|lt=major ('eminent') shrines}} of Suwa district.{{efn|「諏方郡<sub>二座 並大</sub> 南方刀美神社<sub>二座 名神大</sub>」}}<ref>{{cite web|title=Engishiki, vol. 10 (延喜式 第十巻)|url=https://jhti.berkeley.edu/cgi-bin/jhti/image.cgi?page=9&kan=10&honname=3|website=Japanese Historical Text Initiative (JHTI)|access-date=2019-08-23}}</ref> By 940 ({{ill|Tengyō|en|Tengyō|qid=Q1327340|lt=Tengyō}} 3), the deity had been promoted to the highest Rank of senior first (正一位).<ref name="Suwa689" /><ref>{{cite web|title=社家の姓氏-諏訪氏-|url=http://www.harimaya.com/o_kamon1/syake/middle/s_suwa.html|website=播磨屋 (www.harimaya.com)}}</ref>

==Consort and Offspring==

[[File:Suwa taisha akimiya01bs3200.jpg|thumb|left|The ''Akimiya'' (秋宮) or Autumn Shrine, one of the two component shrines of the Suwa ''Shimosha'']]

===Yasakatome===

Suwa Myōjin's spouse is the goddess {{nihongo|'''[[Yasakatome|Yasakatome-no-Kami]]'''|八坂刀売神}}, most often considered to be the deity of the Lower Shrine of Suwa or the ''Shimosha''.<ref>Muraoka (1969). pp. 5–6.</ref> Unlike the relatively well-documented Suwa ''Kamisha'', very little concrete information is available regarding the origins of the ''Shimosha'' and its goddess.<ref>Suwa Shishi Hensan Iinkai, ed. (1995). p. 696.</ref>

[[Yasakatome]]'s first historical attestation is in the ''Shoku Nihon Kōki'', where the goddess is given the Rank of junior fifth, lower grade (従五位下) by the imperial court in the tenth month of {{ill|Jōwa (Heian period)|en|Jōwa (Heian period)|qid=Q1075605|lt=Jōwa}} 9 (842 CE), five months after the same Rank was conferred on Takeminakata.{{efn|「奉授安房國從五位下安房大神正五位下。无位第一后神天比理刀咩命神。信濃國无位健御名方富命前八坂刀賣神。阿波國无位葦稻葉神。越後國无位伊夜比古神。常陸國无位筑波女大神竝從五位下。」}}<ref name="Shoku1" /><ref>{{cite web|title=南方刀美神社二座（八坂刀売命神）|url=http://21coe.kokugakuin.ac.jp/db/jinja/kindex2.php?J_ID=240201|website=神社資料データベース (Shinto Jinja Database)|publisher=Kokugakuin University}}</ref> As Takeminakata rose up in Rank, so did [[Yasakatome]],<ref>Miyasaka (1987). pp. 37-38.</ref><ref name="Montoku" /><ref name="Montoku2" /><ref name="NihonSandai" /> so that by 867 CE, [[Yasakatome]] had been promoted to senior second (正二位).<ref name="NihonSandai2" /> The goddess was finally promoted to senior first Rank (正一位) in 1074 ({{ill|Jōhō|en|Jōhō|qid=Q1193592|lt=Jōhō}} 1).<ref name="Owa221" />

Stories and claims about the goddess are diverse and contradictory. Regarding her parentage for instance, the lore of Kawaai Shrine (川会神社) in [[:en:Kitaazumi District|Kitaazumi District]] identifies [[Yasakatome]] as the daughter of {{ill|Watatsumi|en|Watatsumi|qid=Q1474187|lt=Watatsumi}}, god of the sea,<ref>{{cite web|title=八坂刀売神（ヤサカトメノカミ|url=http://japangod.dip.jp/%E5%85%AB%E5%9D%82%E5%88%80%E5%A3%B2%E7%A5%9E.html|website=日本の神様辞典 (Nihon no Kamisama Jiten)|access-date=May 27, 2017|archive-date=June 25, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170625160608/http://japangod.dip.jp/%E5%85%AB%E5%9D%82%E5%88%80%E5%A3%B2%E7%A5%9E.html|url-status=dead}}</ref>
which has been seen as hinting to a connection between the goddess and the seafaring [[Azumi people|Azumi clan]] ([[:ja:阿曇氏|安曇氏]]).<ref name="Miyasaka39">Miyasaka (1987). p. 39.</ref> Another claim originating from sources dating from the {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|qid=Q184963|lt=Edo period}} is that [[Yasakatome]] was the daughter of Ame-no-yasakahiko (天八坂彦命), a god recorded in the ''Kuji Hongi'' as one of the companions of [[List of Japanese deities#Minor kami|Nigihayahi-no-Mikoto]] when the latter came down from heaven.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Ponsonby-Fane|first1=R. A. B.|title=Studies in Shinto & Shrines|date=2014|publisher=Routledge|isbn=978-1136893018|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=UVO4AwAAQBAJ&pg=PT148}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=先代舊事本紀卷第三 天神本紀|url=https://miko.org/~uraki/kuon/furu/text/sendaikuji/sendaikuji03.htm|website=私本 先代舊事本紀}}</ref><ref name="Miyasaka39" />

The ice cracks that appear on Lake Suwa during cold winters, the ''omiwatari'' ([[#Omiwatari|see above]]) are reputed in folklore to be caused by Suwa Myōjin's crossing the frozen lake to visit [[Yasakatome]].<ref name="railways1922" />

====Princess Kasuga====

The Kōga Saburō legend identifies the goddess of the Shimosha with Saburō's wife, whose name is given in some variants of the story as 'Princess Kasuga' (春日姫 ''Kasuga-hime'').<ref name="SuwaEngi">諏訪縁起の事 (''Suwa engi-no-koto'') in {{cite book|author=Kishi, Shōzō (trans.)|title=Shintōshū (神道集)|series=Tōyō Bunko (東洋文庫) vol. 94|date=1967|publisher=Heibonsha|isbn=978-4-582-80094-4|pages=238–286}}</ref><ref name="Kanai17">Kanai (1982). p. 17.</ref>

===Children===

In Suwa, a number of local deities are popularly considered to be the children of Suwa Myōjin and his consort. Ōta (1926) lists the following gods:<ref name="Ota4445">Ōta (1926). pp. 44–45.</ref>

[[File:Suwa taisha Kamisha Honmiya , 諏訪大社 上社 本宮 - panoramio (19).jpg|thumb|Izuhaya-sha (出早社), an [[Setsumatsusha|auxiliary shrine]] in the ''Kamisha Honmiya'' dedicated to the god Izuhayao (出早雄命), believed to be one of Suwa Myōjin's offspring]]
*Hikokamiwake-no-Mikoto (彦神別命)
*Tatsuwakahime-no-Kami (多都若姫神)
*Tamaru-hime-no-Kami (多留姫神) 
*Izuhayao-no-Mikoto (伊豆早雄命)
*Tateshina-no-Kami (建志名神)
*Tsumashinahime-no-Kami (妻科姫神)
*Ikeno'o-no-Kami (池生神)
*Tsumayamizuhime-no-mMikoto (都麻屋美豆姫命)
*Yakine-no-Mikoto (八杵命)
*Suwa-wakahiko-no-Mikoto (洲羽若彦命)
*Katakurabe-no-Mikoto (片倉辺命)
*Okihagi-no-Mikoto (興波岐命)
*Wakemizuhiko-no-Mikoto (別水彦命)
*Moritatsu-no-Kami (守達神)
*Takamori-no-kami (高杜神)
*Enatakemimi-no-Mikoto (恵奈武耳命)
*Okutsuiwatate-no-Kami (奥津石建神)
*Ohotsuno-no-Kami (竟富角神)
*Ōkunugi-no-Kami (大橡神)

===Claimed descendants===

====Suwa clan====

{{see also|Suwa clan}}

[[File:Jinchoukan-Moriya-shiryoukan_Oohouri-bosho.JPG|thumb|230px|right|The graves of various Suwa ''ōhōri'' within the historical estate grounds of the Moriya clan in Chino, Nagano. Both the [[:ja:神長官守矢史料館|Jinchōkan Moriya Historical Museum]] and the head [[Mishaguji]] shrine (''sōsha'') are located in the same precincts.]]
The [[Suwa clan]] who once occupied the position of head priest or ''ōhōri'' of the Suwa ''Kamisha'' traditionally considered themselves to be descendants of Suwa Myōjin/Takeminakata,<ref name="Picken">{{cite book|last1=Picken|first1=Stuart D.B.|title=Historical Dictionary of Shinto|date=December 28, 2010 |publisher=Scarecrow Press|isbn=978-0-8108-7172-4|page=288|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xlG3F6gSm9UC&pg=PA288}}</ref><ref name="Inoue352">Inoue (2003). p. 352.</ref><ref>{{cite book|author=Rekishi REAL Henshūbu (歴史REAL編集部) (ed.)|title=Jinja to kodai gōzoku no nazo (神社と古代豪族の謎)|date=2016|publisher=Yosensha|isbn=978-4800308924|page=40|language=ja}}</ref> although historically they are probably descended from the Kanasashi-no-toneri clan appointed by the Yamato court to govern the Suwa area in the 6th century ([[#Analysis|see above]]).<ref>Kanai (1982). pp. 14, 106-109.</ref>

====Other clans====

The Suwa ''ōhōri'' was assisted [[Suwa taisha#Kamisha|by five priests]], some of whom were also considered to be descendants of local deities related to Suwa Myōjin/Takeminakata.<ref name="Inoue352" /> One clan, the Koide (小出氏), the original occupants of the offices of ''negi-dayū'' (禰宜大夫) and ''gi-no-hōri'' (擬祝), claimed descent from the god Yakine.<ref>Suwa Shishi Hensan Iinkai, ed. (1995). p. 728, 731.</ref><ref name="Oota1924">{{cite book|author=Ōta, Akira|title=日本國誌資料叢書 信濃 (Nihon kokushi shiryō sōsho: Shinano)|date=1924|location=Tokyo|publisher=Isobe Kōyōdō|url=http://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/982145/84|page=164}}</ref> A second clan, the Yajima (八島(嶋)氏 or 矢島氏), which served as ''gon-no-hōri'' (権祝), considered the god Ikeno'o to be their ancestor.<ref>Suwa Shishi Hensan Iinkai, ed. (1995). p. 730.</ref><ref name="Sasamoto">{{cite book|last1=Sasamoto|first1=Shōji|title=山をめぐる信州史の研究 (Yama wo meguru Shinshū-shi no kenkyū)|date=2003|publisher=Kōshi-shoin|isbn=978-4-906641-66-6|page=72}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=茅野市神長官守矢史料館 (Chino-shi Jinchōkan Moriya Shiryōkan)|url=http://www.suwa-tourism.jp/archives/000733.php|website=信州諏訪観光ナビ}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last1=Ōta|date=1924|title=Nihon kokushi shiryō sōsho: Nagano|page=160}}</ref>

==Worship==
===Shrines===
As the gods of the Grand Shrine of Suwa, Suwa Myōjin/Takeminakata and [[Yasakatome]] also serve as the deities of shrines belonging to the Suwa shrine network (諏訪神社 ''Suwa-jinja'') all over Japan.

===As god of wind and water===

[[File:Nagikama.png|thumb|right|''Nagikama'']]The ''Nihon Shoki''<nowiki />'s record of Yamato emissaries worshipping the god of Suwa alongside the gods of [[Tatsuta Taisha|Tatsuta Shrine]] - worshipped for their power to control and ward off wind-related disasters such as {{ill|Drought|en|Drought|qid=Q43059|lt=Drought}}s and {{ill|Typhoon|en|Typhoon|qid=Q140588|lt=Typhoon}}s<ref>Hall, ed. (1988). p. 531.</ref><ref>{{cite book|last1=Tyler|first1=Royall|title=Japanese No Dramas|date=1992|publisher=Penguin UK|isbn=978-0141907802|page=cclvi|url=https://archive.org/details/japanesendramas0000tyle|url-access=registration}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last1=Bock|first1=Felicia Gressitt|title=Engi-shiki; Procedures of the Engi Era: Books VI-X|date=1972|publisher=Sophia University|page=73}}</ref> - implies that the Yamato imperial court recognized the deity as a god of {{ill|List of wind deities|en|en:List of wind deities|qid=Q51845481|lt=wind}} and {{ill|List of water deities|en|List of water deities|qid=Q13416336|lt=water}} during the late 7th century.<ref name="Yazaki22">{{cite book|editor1-last=Yazaki|editor1-first=Takenori|title=諏訪大社 (Suwa-taisha)|date=1986|publisher=Ginga shobō|series=Ginga gurafikku sensho|volume=4|page=22|language=ja}}</ref><ref name="Muraoka17">Muraoka (1969). p. 17.</ref> One theory regarding the origin of the name '(Take)minakata' even supposes it to derive from a word denoting a body of water (水潟 ''minakata''; [[#Etymology|see above]]).<ref name="Miyasaka31" /><ref name="Okada" /><ref>Suwa Shishi Hensan Iinkai, ed. (1995). p. 686.</ref>

Snake-shaped iron [[:en:Kama (weapon)|sickle]] blades called ''nagikama'' (薙鎌) were traditionally used in the Suwa region to ward off strong winds, typhoons and other natural disasters; it was once customary for ''nagikama'' to be attached to wooden staves and placed on one corner of the rooftop of the house during the autumn typhoon season.<ref name="Yazaki98" /><ref>Miyasaka (1992). pp. 172-173.</ref><ref>Suwa Shishi Hensan Iinkai, ed. (1995). p. 677.</ref> ''Nagikama'' are also traditionally hammered onto the trees chosen to become the ''{{ill|Onbashira|en|Onbashira|qid=Q3698846|lt=Onbashira}}'' of the Suwa ''Kamisha'' and ''Shimosha'' some time before these are actually felled.<ref>Miyasaka (1992). pp. 164-172.</ref> In addition to these and other uses, the blades are also distributed to function as ''[[shintai]]'' for branch shrines of the [[Shinto shrine#Shrine networks|Suwa shrine network]].<ref name="Yazaki98">Yazaki, ed. (1986). pp. 98-100.</ref><ref>Suwa Shishi Hensan Iinkai, ed. (1995). p. 674.</ref>

===Association with snakes and dragons===

Suwa Myōjin's association with the {{ill|Snakes in mythology|en|Snakes in mythology|qid=Q16326794|lt=snake}} or the {{ill|Japanese dragon|en|Japanese dragon|qid=Q2366503|lt=dragon}} in many stories featuring the god such as the Kōga Saburō legend (see [[#Legends of Suwa Myōjin|'Legends of Suwa Myōjin']] above) might be related to his being considered as a deity presiding over wind and water, due to the association of dragons with winds and the rain in Japanese belief.<ref>Kanai (1982). pp. 4-7.</ref><ref>{{cite book|last1=De Visser|first1=Marinus Willem|title=The Dragon in China and Japan|date=1913|page=153|publisher=Cosimo |isbn=9781605204093 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Mpg6Xd2jW2YC&pg=PA153}}</ref> (See also ''[[mizuchi]]''.)

[[File:Samantabhadra_Fugen_Bosatsu_Okura.JPG|thumb|left|170px|Suwa Myōjin was once believed to be a manifestation (''suijaku'') of the bodhisattva Samantabhadra.]]

===Under ''shinbutsu-shūgō''===

During the Middle Ages, under the then-prevalent [[Shinbutsu-shūgō|synthesis of Buddhism and Shinto]], Suwa Myōjin was [[honji suijaku|identified]] with the {{ill|Bodhisattva|en|Bodhisattva|qid=Q178149|lt=Bodhisattva}} {{ill|Samantabhadra (Bodhisattva)|en|Samantabhadra (Bodhisattva)|qid=Q868306|lt=Samantabhadra}} (Fugen),<ref>{{cite book|editor-last1=Yoshii|editor-first1=Yoshitaka |title=えびす信仰事典 (Ebisu shinkō jiten)|date=1999|isbn=978-4-900901-08-7|page=306|publisher=戎光祥出版 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=glXcN9r6GhAC}}</ref><ref>Inoue (2003) p. 354.</ref> with the goddess of the ''Shimosha'' being associated with the [[Avalokiteśvara#Thousand-armed Avalokiteśvara|thousand-armed form of the bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara]] (Senju Kannon).<ref>Miyaji (1931). pp. 75–76.</ref> During the medieval period, {{ill|Jingū-ji|en|Jingū-ji|qid=Q1074971|lt=Buddhist temples and other edifices}} were erected on the precincts of both shrines, including a stone {{ill|Pagoda|en|Pagoda|qid=Q199451|lt=Pagoda}} called the ''Tettō'' (鉄塔 "iron tower") - symbolizing the legendary [[Vajrasattva#Shingon Buddhism|iron tower in India]] where, according to {{ill|Shingon Buddhism|en|Shingon Buddhism|qid=Q550182|lt=Shingon}} tradition, {{ill|Nagarjuna|en|Nagarjuna|qid=Q171195|lt=Nagarjuna}} was said to have received esoteric teachings from {{ill|Vajrasattva|en|Vajrasattva|qid=Q2380086|lt=Vajrasattva}} (who is sometimes identified with Samantabhadra) - and a sanctuary to Samantabhadra (普賢堂 ''Fugendō''), both of which served at the time as the ''Kamisha''<nowiki />'s [[Shintai|main objects of worship]].<ref name="Inoue349350">Inoue (2003). pp. 349-350.</ref>

[[File:Suwa Kamisha Tettō.png|thumb|200px|The ''Kamisha Honmiya''<nowiki />'s Iron Tower or ''Tettō'' photographed during the early 20th century. After the removal or demolition of Buddhist structures in Suwa Shrine following the [[Shinbutsu bunri|separation of Buddhism and Shinto]], this pagoda was moved to Onsenji Temple (温泉寺) in {{ill|Suwa, Nagano|en|Suwa, Nagano|qid=Q846338|lt=Suwa City}}, where it currently resides.]]

With the establishment of {{ill|State Shinto|en|State Shinto|qid=Q1197248|lt=State Shinto}} after the [[Meiji Restoration]] in 1868 and the subsequent [[Shinbutsu bunri|separation of Buddhism and Shinto]], the shrine monks (''shasō'') attached to Buddhist temples in the Suwa shrine complex were laicized, with Buddhist symbols and structures being either removed or destroyed; Buddhist ceremonies performed in both the ''Kamisha'' and the ''Shimosha'', such as the yearly offering of the {{ill|Lotus Sutra|en|en:Lotus Sutra|qid=Q861212|lt=en:Lotus Sutra}} to Suwa Myōjin (involving the placing of a copy of the sutra inside the ''Tettō''), were discontinued.<ref>Inoue (2003). pp. 362-371.</ref>

===As god of hunting===

Suwa Myōjin is also worshipped as a {{ill|List of hunting deities|en|en:List of hunting deities|qid=Q6623822|lt=god of hunting}}; not surprisingly, some of the ''Kamisha''<nowiki />'s religious ceremonies traditionally involve(d) ritual {{ill|Hunting|en|Hunting|qid=Q36963|lt=Hunting}} and/or {{ill|Animal sacrifice|en|Animal sacrifice|qid=Q2142916|lt=Animal sacrifice}}.

For instance, the Frog Hunting Ritual (蛙狩神事 ''kawazugari shinji'') held every New Year's Day involves the shooting (or rather, piercing) of frogs captured from a sacred river or stream within the ''Kamisha''<nowiki />'s precincts with miniature arrows.<ref name="Miyasaka9216">Miyasaka (1992). pp. 16-20.</ref><ref>Yazaki, ed. (1986). p. 72.</ref><ref>Tanigawa (1987). pp. 154-155.</ref> This ritual - which has come under harsh criticism from local activists and animal rights groups for its perceived cruelty to the frogs involved<ref>{{cite web|title=Suwa taisha skewering live frogs (生きたカエルを串刺しにする諏訪大社)|url=http://blog.livedoor.jp/liablog/archives/1790677.html|website=NGO Life Investigation Agency (LIA)|date=December 30, 2013 |access-date=2016-01-05}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Rabid animal rights activists go head-to-head with tradition|url=https://japantoday.com/Category/features/kuchikomi/rabid-animal-rights-activists-go-head-to-head-with-tradition|website=Japan Today|date=September 30, 2015 }}</ref> - was traditionally performed to secure peace and a bountiful harvest for the coming year.<ref name="Miyasaka9216" />

Another festival, the ''Ontōsai'' (御頭祭) or the ''Tori no matsuri'' (酉の祭, so called because it was formerly held on the {{ill|Earthly Branches|en|Earthly Branches|qid=Q1072961|lt=Day of}} {{ill|Rooster (zodiac)|en|Rooster (zodiac)|qid=Q822621|lt=the Rooster}}) currently held every April 15, feature the offering of seventy-five {{ill|Taxidermy|en|Taxidermy|qid=Q243237|lt=stuffed deer heads}} (a substitute for freshly cut heads of deer used in the past), as well as the consumption of {{ill|Venison|en|Venison|qid=Q2296872|lt=Venison}} and other {{ill|Game (hunting)|en|Game (hunting)|qid=Q223930|lt=game}} such as {{ill|Wild boar|en|Wild boar|qid=Q58697|lt=Wild boar}} or {{ill|Rabbit|en|Rabbit|qid=Q9394|lt=Rabbit}}, various kinds of seafood and other foodstuffs by the priests and other participants in a ritual banquet.<ref>Miyasaka (1992). pp. 69-72.</ref><ref>Yazaki, ed. (1986). pp. 74-75.</ref><ref>Oh (2011). pp. 173-175.</ref><ref>Tanigawa (1987). pp. 155-156.</ref><ref>Fujimori, Terunobu (1991). ''Maemiya Jikkenrō de no saishi'' (前宮十間廊での祭祀). In Jinchōkan Moriya Historical Museum, ed. pp. 15–17.</ref>

One of the Suwa ''Kamisha''<nowiki />'s hunting festivals, the Misayama Festival (御射山祭), formerly held in a field - the ''kōya'' (神野 'the god's plain') - at the foot of the [[Yatsugatake Mountains]] for five days (from the 26th to the 30th of [[Japanese calendar#Months|the seventh month]]),{{efn|Currently three days: from the 26th to the 28th of August.<ref>Tanigawa (1987). p. 157.</ref>}} was one of the grandest festivals in Suwa during the {{ill|Kamakura period|en|Kamakura period|qid=Q236205|lt=Kamakura period}}, attracting many of the {{ill|Samurai|en|Samurai|qid=Q38142|lt=samurai class}} from all across Japan who engaged in displays of [[Yabusame|mounted archery]], bouts of [[:en:Sumo wrestling|Sumo wrestling]] and {{ill|Takagari|en|Takagari|qid=Q16933847|lt=falconry}} as part of the festivities, as well as people from all walks of life.<ref>Tanigawa (1987). pp. 159-160.</ref><ref>Yazaki, ed. (1986). pp. 76-77.</ref><ref>Miyasaka (1992). pp. 115-118.</ref> The ''Shimosha'' also held its own Misayama Festival at the same time as the ''Kamisha'' (albeit in a different location), in which various warrior clans also participated.<ref>Tanigawa (1987). pp. 158-159.</ref><ref>Miyasaka (1992). pp. 119-124.</ref>

Suwa Myōjin's association with the mountains and hunting is also evident from the description of the ''ōhōri'' as sitting upon a deer hide (the deer being an animal thought to be sacred to Suwa Myōjin) during the ''Ontōsai'' ritual as practiced during medieval times.<ref>Tanigawa (1987). p. 138.</ref><ref>Oh (2011). pp. 173.</ref>

====Suwa Myōjin and meat eating====

At a time when slaughter of animals and consumption of meat was frowned upon due to {{ill|Mahayana|en|Mahayana|qid=Q48362|lt=Mahayana}}'s [[Buddhist vegetarianism#Mahayana view|strict views on vegetarianism]] and [[Buddhist ethics#Killing|the general Buddhist opposition against the taking of life]], the cult of Suwa Myōjin was a unique feature in the Japanese religious landscape for its celebration of hunting and meat eating.<ref>Kanai (1982). p. 21-23.</ref>

A four-line verse attached to the Kōga Saburō legend popularly known as the ''Suwa no kanmon'' (諏訪の勘文) encapsulates the justification of meat eating within a Buddhist framework: by being eaten by humans and 'dwelling' inside their bodies, ignorant animals could achieve {{ill|Enlightenment in Buddhism|en|Enlightenment in Buddhism|qid=Q1137019|lt=enlightenment}} together with their human consumers.<ref>Kanai (1982). p. 22.</ref><ref>Miyasaka (1987). pp. 56-57.</ref>

{{Blockquote|text=<poem>業尽有情 ''Gōjin ujō''
雖放不生 ''Suihō fushō''
故宿人天 ''Koshuku ninten''
同証仏果 ''Dōshō bukka''<ref name="SuwaEngi" /><ref>See Kanai (1982). pp. 318-319 for attested variants.</ref>

Sentient beings who have exhausted their {{ill|Karma in Buddhism|en|Karma in Buddhism|qid=Q2673416|lt=karma}}:
Even if one [[Animals in Buddhism#Release of animals|sets (them) free]], (they) will not live (for long);
Therefore (have them) dwell within humans and {{ill|Deva (Buddhism)|en|Deva (Buddhism)|qid=Q4089509|lt=gods}}
(That they may) as well achieve {{ill|Buddhahood|en|Buddhahood|qid=Q56247062|lt=Buddhahood}}</poem>}}

The ''Kamisha'' produced special talismans (鹿食免 ''kajiki-men'' "permit to eat {{ill|Venison|en|Venison|qid=Q2296872|lt=Venison}}") and {{ill|Chopsticks|en|Chopsticks|qid=Q81980|lt=Chopsticks}} (鹿食箸 ''kajiki-bashi'') that were held to allow the bearer to eat meat.<ref name="EOSsuwashinko">{{cite web|last1=Nogami|first1=Takahiro|title=Suwa Shinkō|url=http://k-amc.kokugakuin.ac.jp/DM/dbSearchList.do?class_name=col_eos&search_condition_type=1&db_search_condition_type=4&View=2&startNo=1&focus_type=0&searchFreeword=Suwa%20Shink%C5%8D&searchRangeType=0|website=Encyclopedia of Shinto|publisher=Kokugakuin University|access-date=May 27, 2017|archive-date=April 29, 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180429025336/http://k-amc.kokugakuin.ac.jp/DM/dbSearchList.do?class_name=col_eos&search_condition_type=1&db_search_condition_type=4&View=2&startNo=1&focus_type=0&searchFreeword=Suwa%20Shink%C5%8D&searchRangeType=0|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name="Miyasaka5556">Miyasaka (1987). pp. 55-56.</ref><ref>{{cite web|last1=Uehara|first1=Yoshiko|title=Revival of Japan's Wild Game Cuisine|url=http://www.nippon.com/en/views/b01712/|website=nippon.com|date=April 3, 2015 }}</ref><ref name="Kajikimen">''Kajikimen'' (鹿食免). In Jinchōkan Moriya Historical Museum, ed. (1991). pp. 27–28.</ref> Since it was the only one of its kind in Japan, the talisman was popular among hunters and meat eaters.<ref name="Inoue352"/> These sacred licenses and chopsticks were distributed to the public both by the priests of the ''Kamisha'' as well as wandering preachers associated with the shrine known as ''oshi'' (御師), who preached the tale of Suwa Myōjin as Kōga Saburō as well as other stories concerning the god and his benefits.<ref name="Inoue352" /><ref name="Kajikimen" />

===As war god===
[[File:Hatajirushi3.png|180px|thumb|right|A depiction of war banners used by the [[Taira clan]] (right) and Takeda Shingen (left). The leftmost banner (white with blue border and red lettering) carries the inscription ''Suwa hosshō-kamishimo-daimyōjin'' (諏訪法性上下大明神).]]
[[File:Shingen_Takeda%27s_armour.jpg|180px|thumb|right|A modern reproduction of Takeda Shingen's helmet]]
Suwa Myōjin is also considered to be a {{ill|List of war deities|en|List of war deities|qid=Q1752560|lt=god of war}}, one of a number of such deities in the Japanese pantheon. Besides the legend of the god's apparition to [[Sakanoue no Tamuramaro]] ([[#Apparition to Sakanoue no Tamuramaro|see above]]), the ''[[:en:Songs to Make the Dust Dance on the Beams|Ryōjin Hishō]]'' compiled in 1179 (the late {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|qid=Q193292|lt=Heian period}}) also attest to the worship of the god of Suwa in the capacity of god of warfare at the time of its compilation, naming the shrine of Suwa among famous shrines to martial deities in the eastern half of the country.

{{Blockquote|text=<poem>These gods of war live [[:en:Kantō|east of the barrier]]:{{efn|During the Heian period, the expression 'east of the barrier' (関の東 ''seki-no-hi(n)gashi'', whence derives the term 関東 ''Kantō'') referred to the provinces beyond the checkpoints or barrier stations (関 ''seki'') at the eastern fringes of {{ill|Kinai|en|Kinai|qid=Q906708|lt=the capital region}}, more specifically the land east of the checkpoint at Ōsaka/Ausaka Hill (逢坂 'hill of meeting', old orthography: ''Afusaka''; not to be confused with the modern city of {{ill|Osaka|en|Osaka|qid=Q35765|lt=Osaka}}) in modern {{ill|Ōtsu|en|Ōtsu|qid=Q202907|lt=Ōtsu}}, {{ill|Shiga Prefecture|en|Shiga Prefecture|qid=Q131358|lt=Shiga Prefecture}}.<ref name="books.google.com">{{cite book|last1=Marshall|first1=Yuko|title=Heterogeneous Japan: The Cultural Distinctions Between Western and Eastern Japan|date=2008|page=6|isbn=9780549562146|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=8EdvhO4Xkn4C&pg=PA6|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170215161620/https://books.google.com/books?id=8EdvhO4Xkn4C&pg=PA6|url-status=dead|archive-date=February 15, 2017}}</ref> By the Edo period, ''Kantō'' was reinterpreted to mean the region east of the checkpoint in {{ill|Hakone|en|Hakone|qid=Q671040|lt=Hakone}}, {{ill|Kanagawa Prefecture|en|Kanagawa Prefecture|qid=Q127513|lt=Kanagawa Prefecture}}.}}
[[Kashima Jingū|Kashima]], [[Katori Jingū|Katori]], Suwa no Miya, and [[Shirahige Shrine|Hira Myōjin]];
also [[Awa Shrine|Su]] in {{ill|Awa Province (Chiba)|en|Awa Province (Chiba)|qid=Q1053044|lt=Awa}}, [[:ja:下立松原神社|Otaka Myōjin]] in {{ill|Shirahama, Chiba|en|Shirahama, Chiba|qid=Q1951937|lt=Tai no Kuchi}},
[[Kusanagi no Tsurugi|Yatsurugi]] in [[:en:Atsuta Jingu|Atsuta]], and [[Tado Taisha|Tado no Miya]] in {{ill|Ise Province|en|Ise Province|qid=Q864166|lt=Ise}}.</poem>|title=''Ryōjin Hishō''|source=song 258<ref name="University of California Press">{{cite book|last1=Kim|first1=Yung-Hee|title=Songs to Make the Dust Dance: The Ryōjin Hishō of Twelfth-century Japan|date=1994|publisher=University of California Press|location=Berkeley|isbn=978-0-520-08066-9|pages=144–145a|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=SFlSLX-nCeEC&pg=PA144}}</ref> {{efn|「関より東(ひむかし)の軍神(いくさがみ)、鹿島・香取(かんどり)・諏訪の宮、また比良(ひら)の明神、安房の洲(す)滝(たい)の口や小鷹明神、熱田に八剣(やつるぎ)、伊勢には多度(たど)の宮。」}}}}

During the Kamakura period, the Suwa clan's association with the {{ill|Kamakura shogunate|en|Kamakura shogunate|qid=Q736839|lt=shogunate}} and the {{ill|Hōjō clan|en|Hōjō clan|qid=Q834364|lt=Hōjō clan}} helped further cement Suwa Myōjin's reputation as a martial deity.<ref name="Yazaki25">Yazaki (1986). p. 25.</ref> The shrines of Suwa and the priestly clans thereof flourished under the patronage of the Hōjō, which promoted devotion to the god as a sign of loyalty to the shogunate.<ref name="Yazaki25" /> Suwa branch shrines became numerous all across Japan, especially in territories held by clans devoted to the god (for instance, the {{ill|Kantō region|en|Kantō region|qid=Q132480|lt=Kantō region}}, traditional stronghold of the [[Minamoto clan|Minamoto]] ({{ill|Seiwa Genji|en|Seiwa Genji|qid=Q2164991|lt=Seiwa Genji}}) clan).<ref>Muraoka (1969). p. 112.</ref>

The [[Takeda clan]] of {{ill|Kai Province|en|Kai Province|qid=Q858076|lt=Kai Province}} (modern {{ill|Yamanashi Prefecture|en|Yamanashi Prefecture|qid=Q132720|lt=Yamanashi Prefecture}}) were devotees of Suwa Myōjin, its most famous member, the Sengoku ''daimyō'' {{ill|Takeda Shingen|en|Takeda Shingen|qid=Q276404|lt=Takeda Shingen}} being no exception.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Katō|first1=Aki|title=写真と絵でわかる 古事記・日本書紀 (Shashin to e de wakaru Kojiki - Nihon Shoki)|date=2015|publisher=Seitōsha|isbn=978-4791620661|page=59|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=dQXIBgAAQBAJ&pg=PA59}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=信玄の信仰 (Shingen no shinkō)|url=http://home.d03.itscom.net/p-l514/syukyou.html|website=Takeda Shingenの館 (Takeda Shingen no yakata)}}</ref> His devotion is visibly evident in some of his war banners, which bore the god's name and invocations such as ''Namu Suwa Nangū Hosshō Kamishimo Daimyōjin'' (南無諏方南宮法性上下大明神 '{{ill|Namaste|en|Namaste|qid=Q60653|lt=Namo}} Dharma-Nature ''Daimyōjin'' of the Suwa Upper and Lower Shrines').<ref name="Guide"/> The iconic horned {{ill|Kabuto|en|Kabuto|qid=Q1720878|lt=helmet}} with the flowing white hair commonly associated with Shingen, popularly known as the ''Suwa-hosshō'' helmet (諏訪法性兜 ''Suwa-hosshō-(no)-kabuto''), came to be reputed in some popular culture retellings to have been blessed by the god, guaranteeing success in battle to its wearer.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Brandon|first1=James R.|last2=Leiter|first2=Samuel L. (eds.)|title=Kabuki Plays on Stage: Brilliance and Bravado, 1697–1766, Volume 1|date=2002|publisher=University of Hawaii Press|isbn=978-0-8248-2403-7|page=328|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=VfB18HqorrwC&pg=PA328}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last1=Gessel|first1=Van C.|last2=Rimer|first2=J. Thomas|title=The Columbia Anthology of Modern Japanese Literature: From Restoration to Occupation, 1868–1945|date=2010|publisher=Columbia University Press|isbn=978-0-231-52164-2|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=8p6oUV9ln6cC&pg=PA138|page=138}}</ref> Shingen also issued an order for the reinstitution of the religious rites of both the ''Kamisha'' and the ''Shimosha'' in 1565.<ref>Tanigawa (1987). p. 137.</ref><ref>Yazaki (1986). p. 26.</ref>
